contradictions.issue: The one rule the whole book exists to enforce — the wordmark's word space — is specified four different ways. Verbal: "letter tracking of 0.40 em", "minimum of 1.0 em", "never less than 2.5× the gap between two letters", CSS `letter-spacing: 0.40em; word-spacing: 0.60em`. Visual: "+320/1000 em (0.32 em)", "+0.96 em minimum", "≥ 3.0×", CSS `letter-spacing: 0.32em; word-spacing: 0.64em`. Applications: "the word space must be set at 3× the letter tracking value". Motion: "the word gap baked in at a fixed 0.62em" and an intro that animates "letterspacing 0.38em → 0.32em". A book whose thesis is one source of truth contains four sources of truth for its own headline rule.
contradictions.resolution: Pick Visual's numbers (0.32 em / 0.96 em / 3.0×) as the only ones, delete the CSS block and the values from Verbal §6.1–6.2 and from Applications §0, and replace them with a cross-reference to §3.1.6. Also delete the Motion letterspacing animation outright: Visual misuse rules 6 and 8 forbid re-setting or re-tracking the wordmark, so the brand cannot animate its tracking in its own title sequence.

contradictions.issue: Wordmark minimum size is stated three incompatible ways. Visual: "OUR TIME wordmark — 128 px … 32 mm litho … 40 mm screen print on fabric". Applications: "the wordmark has a minimum reproduction width of 120mm on garment; below that, use the monogram". Motion: "Minimum render width for the wordmark: 132 px on web". 40 mm and 120 mm are not a rounding difference — one of them allows a chest wordmark and the other bans it.
contradictions.resolution: Applications is right on the physics and Visual is wrong: a 40 mm wordmark on washed heavyweight cotton has sub-0.4 mm stems. Set 120 mm as the garment minimum in §3.1.4, keep 32 mm for litho on smooth stock, keep 132 px for screen (and correct Visual's 128 px to match), and state the substrate next to every number.

contradictions.issue: Three different launch ranges. Strategy: "Recommended launch cut: ~14 SKUs" including two polos, two shorts, the sweatpant and the jean. Commercial: "Drop one: make this. Three garment types. Six colourways. 320 units" and explicitly cuts jeans, all polos and all shorts. Verbal's worked drop announcement says "Seven tees, five polos, four crews, four hoodies" and its worked email preheader says "Twenty-eight pieces. Seven garments. One drop." The founder is given three launch plans and no instruction on which one is the plan.
contradictions.resolution: Commercial wins — it is the only version with the arithmetic attached. Rewrite Strategy §7.20 to the six-colourway drop and rewrite Verbal's worked examples to match it ("Two tees, two hoodies, one crew, one sweatpant"). Every worked example in the book should use drop one's actual contents, so the founder can copy them.

contradictions.issue: The price architecture disagrees with itself by up to 25%. Strategy: crewneck "£85–95", zip hoodie "£95–110". Commercial: crew "£75", zip hoodie "£85". Verbal's worked order-confirmation email then prices "0600 CREW — Cream, L £85", which matches neither. The cited competitor evidence also conflicts: Strategy says "Cole Buxton hoodies are £175", Commercial says "£139 hoodie / £159 zip hoodie" from the same brand's own site.
contradictions.resolution: Commercial's figures are the only ones tied to landed cost — adopt £75/£85 everywhere, correct Verbal's email, and delete the Strategy price table in favour of a pointer to Commercial §1.3. Re-check the Cole Buxton prices once and quote one number.

contradictions.issue: Pillar 1 states the rule: "one brand mark per garment as the rule (chest OT *or* a back-print, not both)". Commercial then costs the hero tee as "Oversized heavyweight tee (back print + chest) … Decoration 7.00 (2 applications)" — a garment the brand book forbids — and uses that £24.85 landed cost for both drop-one tees, which are described as back-print only ("Navy — hourglass back-print", "White — wordmark back-print"). Commercial §1.4 then recommends "Print less on the tee. One print position, not two" as if it were a new idea rather than an existing rule.
contradictions.resolution: Delete the two-application tee from §1.3. Drop one's tees are one application at £21.35 landed, which takes the multiple to 2.34× and the drop-one buy to roughly £8,470, not £8,956. Fix the totals — they are currently quoted to the pound.

contradictions.issue: Strategy: "No accent colour is ever introduced" and, in the NOT list, "No accent colour." Visual: "**Accent (the only one)** `#54647E` Washed Denim — links, active states, data marks, the coordinate line, the one thing on a page allowed to be a colour." Motion then spends its only saturated pixel on the same hex. Strategy means "no *new* accent" but does not say so, and a founder reading the NOT list will strike Visual's link colour.
contradictions.resolution: Rewrite the Strategy lines to "One accent exists — #54647E. No second one is ever introduced, and nothing above C* 20 enters the palette." Also note the collision Visual misses: #54647E is simultaneously a garment colourway (1600 SHORT), so the UI accent and a product colour are the same value.

contradictions.issue: "No third typographic voice. Heavy italic OT and thin wide wordmark. That's the whole system" (Strategy), echoed by Visual: "A third voice is not permitted." Visual §3.3.2 then buys three families — Druk Wide display, GT America text, GT America Mono — and §3.3.4 gives the mono two dedicated tokens carrying coordinates, EST. 2026 and captions. That is four voices on the page by the book's own counting method, introduced two pages after the ban.
contradictions.resolution: Say what is actually meant: the *logo* has two voices; the typographic system has three roles (display, text, mono) and the mono exists to carry numbers. Then fix the knock-on: coordinates are specified in the mono (Visual §3.4.3b), in "the wordmark face" (Motion §2.1, §7.3) and in "the thin wide-tracked wordmark face" (Applications §2.2). Pick one, and stop calling the wordmark a "face" — it is outlined artwork, and calling it a typeface is exactly how a supplier ends up typing it.

contradictions.issue: Strategy: the OVERTIME pieces are "never sold, never photographed, never listed, and never turned into a cute 'misprint drop' story." Commercial §7.2: "Do not sell them. Not at a discount, not as seconds, not quietly." Visual's own open-items table then instructs the founder to "Recall/relabel or **sell through** the existing OVERTIME garments **as a deliberate, named first-run anomaly** — decide which, in writing, once." The book bans the misprint-drop story twice and then sets it as a to-do.
contradictions.resolution: Delete Visual open item 6 and replace it with the decision already made: "OVERTIME stock is destroyed or given away unlisted and unphotographed. Archive the files in 99_ARCHIVE. No further decision required."

contradictions.issue: Verbal specifies the 404: heading "THIS HOUR IS EMPTY.", body, link "THE INDEX", and the instruction "Do not put a joke here. Do not put an hourglass here. **Do not animate anything here.**" Motion specifies the same page as "320px, vortex **on**, compass star with the Black Isle coordinates. Copy: **TIME WON'T WAIT.** … This is the only page allowed to be indulgent." Two different headings and opposite motion rules for one page.
contradictions.resolution: Motion's version is the better page and the vortex costs nothing on a dead end — but the book has to choose. Keep the Mechanism with vortex, keep Verbal's heading ("THIS HOUR IS EMPTY." is a better line than a reused tagline), and rewrite Verbal §3.9 to say so.

contradictions.issue: Verbal: "The CTA vocabulary is fixed and short: `SEE THE INDEX` · `VIEW THE DROP` · `BUY` · `SET A REMINDER`. **Never `SHOP NOW`.**" Applications' drop email then uses "`SHOP NOW →` button, above the fold", a second `SHOP NOW →` lower down, and a third in the back-in-stock email.
contradictions.resolution: Replace all three with `VIEW THE DROP →` and `BUY →`. This is a one-line fix, but it is the clearest example of two sections written without reading each other — worth flagging to the founder as the reason a single owner has to sign off the whole book.

contradictions.issue: Motion's anti-list: "Never: … Any countdown, drop timer, or 'scarcity' clock." Applications: "A countdown Story sticker on the 24 hours before an actual drop is fine — that is real scarcity." Commercial: "**Show units remaining, truthfully** … A counter that says 87 of 120 is more persuasive than a clock." A live depleting counter is the same psychological mechanic Motion bans absolutely, and the book never reconciles "no clocks" with "real deadlines are allowed".
contradictions.resolution: State the actual principle once, in Strategy: *the brand may state a fact that happens to be urgent; it may never animate urgency.* Then: run size on the page yes; units remaining yes, updated on page load, never ticking; a 24-hour Story sticker before a real drop yes; a timer in the site chrome or an email never. Amend Motion's absolute ban to "never in the Mechanism, never in the site chrome, never in email".

contradictions.issue: Three different care instructions for the same garments. Verbal's care-label voice block says "HANG DRY." Commercial's on-page disclosure says "Wash cold, inside out. Hang dry. **Do not tumble dry.**" Applications' literal care-label wording block says "**TUMBLE DRY LOW**". On garment-dyed heavyweight cotton with a residual 1–3% shrinkage, that is the difference between a fitting garment and a return — and the wrong version is the one going on the physical label.
contradictions.resolution: Delete "TUMBLE DRY LOW" from the Applications block and align all three to: WASH COLD 30° · INSIDE OUT · DO NOT BLEACH · **DO NOT TUMBLE DRY** · COOL IRON, NOT ON PRINT · DO NOT DRY CLEAN. One block, reproduced identically in all three sections or, better, in one and referenced twice.

contradictions.issue: Visual's ground-assignment rule permanently assigns navy (#141B2C, 1.12:1) and washed black (#171717, 1.07:1) to the PAPER ground #DFDDDE, and says a mixed grid "is *correct*, not broken." Applications then specifies near-black for all product photography — Instagram "Dead-on, soft top light, near-black ground", lookbook pp.6–13 "flat-lay (dead-on, soft top light, `#0F0F0F` ground)" — and Commercial proposes cutting "Any colourway you cannot photograph well" on the grounds of that same 1.07:1 figure. Drop one is navy tee, navy hoodie and washed-black sweatpant: four of six pieces are paper-ground garments that every other section shoots on black.
contradictions.resolution: Visual's rule is the best thinking in the photography direction and the other two sections have not absorbed it. Propagate it: rewrite the Applications flat-lay spec and the lookbook sequence to "ground per §3.2.5", and delete Commercial §2.5's cut criterion — the answer to an invisible navy is a paper ground, not a cancelled colourway.

contradictions.issue: Visual: the two navies "may **never** appear in the same photograph, flat-lay set, or product grid. If the navy tee and the navy short are shown together, one of them is the wrong navy and a customer will notice on arrival." Verbal's ledger then gives both hexes the same name — "both remain 2200 NAVY" — and §4.9 merchandises "**THE 2200 SET** — navy. Two tees, polo, crew, hoodie, short", which is precisely the forbidden photograph, sold as a set.
contradictions.resolution: Either kill one navy before the next buy (Visual's own open item 2, which should be promoted to a drop-one blocker) or split the ledger: 2200 NAVY jersey and 2100 NAVY woven, with no set that crosses them. The current position — same name, different colour, never shown together, sold as a head-to-toe set — cannot survive a single customer order.

contradictions.issue: Two specs for the two objects the customer actually holds. Swing tag front: Verbal says "the lockup only. OT monogram above, OUR TIME wordmark below, `EST. 2026` beneath"; Applications says "**OT monogram**, 26mm wide, centred … Nothing else. No tagline, no URL, no 'EST. 2026'." Neck label: Verbal says the hour "goes on the internal neck label, **under the wordmark**, small"; Applications says "**OT monogram only. Not the wordmark**" — with a good reason (thread cannot hold hairlines) that Verbal has not heard.
contradictions.resolution: Applications is right on both, for manufacturing reasons. Rewrite Verbal §3.8 to a monogram-only tag front and move the hour to sit under the monogram on the neck label. Then reconcile the tag backs, which are also two different layouts (Verbal has product name and colour, Applications has a QR and a URL).

contradictions.between: verbal §4.3 ledger rule / verbal §4.8 jean row
contradictions.issue: The ledger's own rule: "A colour's hour is assigned once and never changes. To add a colour, take a free hour; **never reuse or reassign one**." The range table then assigns `0300` to both Washed Black `#171717` and, on the jean, "Washed Black Denim" with a separate unmeasured hex. Two different colours, one hour, in the table that defines the rule — and the 0300 SET is then sold as "one colour" across six pieces including the jean.
contradictions.resolution: Give the denim its own free hour (0200 reads correctly for a darker, bluer black) and remove the jean from "THE 0300 SET". Otherwise the first system in the book breaks on the first page it is applied to.

contradictions.issue: Commercial: "**S, M, L, XL, XXL.** Five sizes, no more, for drop one. No XS, no 3XL until demand tells you." Applications: "buy one care-label SKU per size … That is **seven sizes** × one artwork, not 31 SKUs." The founder is ordering labels off the wrong number.
contradictions.resolution: Five, and say it once. This is a live purchasing error — labels get ordered in weeks 6–7 of the launch plan, before anyone re-reads the sizing section.

contradictions.issue: Verbal's mechanics table: "Time format — 24-hour, four digits, leading zero, **no colon**: `0600`, not `6:00am`", reinforced in §4.2: "The colon is deliberately withheld — it reads as a running clock." Visual then specifies the dial: "The hands are **locked at 07:24** on every appearance". The brand's own clock face is set in the one time format the brand bans.
contradictions.resolution: Write it `0724` in every brief and every file name, and state the dial's time as "hands at 0724". Trivial, but it is the kind of inconsistency that reaches a printer.

contradictions.between: strategy §2 table and pillar 1 / verbal §5 usage rules / visual §3.3.4 and §3.6.5
contradictions.issue: Strategy sets the structural rule: "**The thin wordmark carries process copy. The heavy monogram carries arrival.**" Verbal enforces it: "Print lines in the **thin wordmark weight**, wide-tracked, never in the heavy monogram style." Visual's type scale then makes `D1` "Display, Bold Italic" with the example "TIME WON'T WAIT.", and the worked hero sets "`D1` \"EARN EVERY SECOND.\" in Display Bold Italic" — process copy in the loud voice — while the OT monogram sits in the header of the same view, breaking Verbal §0's "Never shout twice."
contradictions.resolution: Decide whether the heavy display face is allowed to carry process copy at all. Cleanest answer: it is not. Set grind-half lines in the text face at wordmark tracking, reserve `D1` Bold Italic for arrival lines (`OUR TIME.`, drop names, the 0300 SET), and rewrite the §3.6.5 hero accordingly — it is the one worked example a founder will copy.

contradictions.issue: Strategy: "There is no founder cult. The client is not the brand's protagonist" and "Copy is written in first person plural." Applications' welcome email specifies "**Three to four short paragraphs, first person, from the founder.** Where the Black Isle is. Why the brand is called OUR TIME", and the thank-you card carries "Two or three sentences from the founder, **written by him**". Verbal §3.6 also bans "false intimacy" in email.
contradictions.resolution: These are reconcilable but not as written. Rule: the founder may write, in the first person, about *facts he is the only witness to* — the dye bath, the first run, the weather on the shoot day — and never about himself, his journey, or what the brand means. Add that sentence to Pillar 3 and cap the welcome email at two paragraphs.

contradictions.issue: Verbal's order-confirmation email promises "Wrong size, wrong colour, wrong decision: 30 days, unworn, **tags on**." Commercial's legal section warns: "**Do not write:** 'no returns on sale items', '**no returns without original packaging**', 'returns within 7 days', or 'store credit only'. For distance cancellations, all four are unenforceable." A tags-on condition is the same class of unenforceable condition, printed in the brand's most-sent email.
contradictions.resolution: Rewrite to the lawful version: "30 days, in the condition you'd have handled it in a shop. Reply to this email and we'll sort it." Keep the right to deduct for diminished value, and say that in the policy page rather than the receipt.

contradictions.issue: Verbal: "**Special case — `24 / 7`.** It is a mark, not a sentence … **not permitted in body copy, subject lines or social captions**", and the tagline bank marks it "**A only**". Applications' Instagram post-type table then lists the mechanism graphic as "Rotate: `EARN EVERY SECOND.` / `TIME WON'T WAIT.` / `DISCIPLINE. FOCUS. CONSISTENCY.` / **`24 / 7`**" — a social post consisting of the mark alone — and Visual's `LABEL` token lists "24 / 7" among its permitted uses.
contradictions.resolution: Delete 24 / 7 from the Applications rotation and from the LABEL examples. It flanks the globe, it labels the two orbit nodes in the Mechanism, and it appears nowhere else — which is the only thing keeping it from reading as the grind-culture cliché the brand is trying to escape.

contradictions.issue: Visual: "**Rule 3.4.1a — One motif per garment.** No garment carries two." The baggy jean carries the all-over OT pattern (rank 1) *and* the Roman-numeral clock-face pocket print (rank 2), in the existing artwork, in the Applications method table and in the range listing. Strategy calls the all-over jean "the deliberate exception that proves" the one-mark rule but never addresses the second motif.
contradictions.resolution: Either write the exception properly — "the jean carries the pattern as a wash treatment, which does not count as a motif; the pocket dial is its one motif" — or drop the pocket print. As drafted, the brand's flagship piece breaks a rule stated two sections earlier, and the founder has no way to know which is intended.

contradictions.issue: Strategy is emphatic: "Casting is **groups**, never a single hero model looking hard at the camera" and "campaign casting is groups, never a lone hero." Visual's on-body direction is written entirely for one person — "Camera at the subject's chest-to-eye height", "Standing, walking, hands in pockets", "Full-length, or three-quarter cropped at mid-thigh", "One tight crop per look" — with no group framing, no spacing rule and no guidance on how a group shot is composed. Applications then plans it as "Needs a friend and 20 minutes of decent light", i.e. two people, which is neither.
contradictions.resolution: Add a group spec to §3.5.2: minimum two, maximum four, nobody centred, at least one person not looking at the camera, and a lens/distance for a group (35 mm at full-length breaks down past three people). Otherwise the founder shoots exactly what Pillar 3 bans, because it is the only thing the photography section tells him how to shoot.

contradictions.issue: Motion's central claim is that the animated object and the printed object are one: "The Mechanism is not a *Doctor Who* homage bolted onto the brand. It is the back-print of the globe tee and the pocket print of the jeans, turning", and "the animated object and the print object were **the same object**." They are not. The printed dial has hands, locked at 07:24, with OT replacing XII. The Mechanism has no hands at all, a rotating numeral ring, a 60-tick escapement, a 30-tooth bezel and two orbits, with "the heavy XII is the hand." A customer seeing both sees two different marks.
contradictions.resolution: Make the claim true or drop it. The cheap fix: derive the printed dial from the settled frame — same numeral set, same OT at twelve, hands at the angles the settled frame implies — and publish it as one file in `04_MOTIFS/` used for the sticker, the pocket print and the animation's frame zero. That also solves Applications' seal-sticker problem, which currently needs a separate simplified cut.

contradictions.issue: The daylight fact is the strategy's single strongest piece of evidence and the book quotes it three ways. Strategy: "the shortest **6 hours 41 minutes**". Visual §3.5.3: "In December the sun is up around **09:00 and down around 15:30**" (6h30, consistent). Visual §3.4.3: "**nine hours of usable winter daylight**". Nine hours is wrong by nearly half a working day, in the section that governs the artwork carrying the coordinates.
contradictions.resolution: Fix §3.4.3 to 6h41m and lock the two numbers (18h07m / 6h41m) into the fact sheet as protected values alongside the coordinates and the spelling, since they are the brand's only quantitative claim about itself.

cliches.section: strategy §7.15, motion §3 ("IT KEEPS TIME, IT DOESN'T SELL IT"), applications §7.2
cliches.item: "Scarcity that's always on isn't scarcity, it's a Shopify app" — the same punchline three times, near-verbatim.
cliches.replace_with: State the rule once, in Commercial §4.2, as an instruction: "No timer anywhere. Publish the run size and the number left. Both are facts and neither resets at midnight." Delete the joke from the other two sections.

cliches.item: Pillar names in the X-not-Y formula: "Earned, not announced" · "Time you can feel" · "Our, not my" · "Consistency is the product". This is the single most templated construction in brand strategy and none of the four names tells anyone what to do.
cliches.replace_with: Name each pillar with the rule it enforces: "One mark per garment" · "Dated to real light" · "Cast in twos and threes" · "Nothing ships unchecked". The "so what" paragraphs already contain these — promote them and delete the aphorisms.

cliches.item: "Everything in this price bracket looks like it came from nowhere. Ours came from somewhere, and we can prove it." Deck-speak, and the brand cannot currently prove it — the proof is an unverified biographical claim.
cliches.replace_with: The proof itself, stated flat: "Shot on the Black Isle in December, at 57.5878° N, 4.2383° W." If that sentence cannot be made true this year, the positioning line has to change, not the rhetoric.

cliches.item: "NOBODY HANDS YOU THE HOUR." · "SET YOUR OWN HOUR." · "SECONDS ARE CHEAP. HOURS AREN'T." · "KEEP YOUR OWN TIME." — four new lines in exactly the motivational-fragment register §1.3 exists to ban. They assert rather than observe, which is the test the section sets itself ("`SHOW UP.` is a command from a stranger. `THE HOURS SHOW.` is an observation").
cliches.replace_with: Lines only the Black Isle could produce: "LIGHT UNTIL ELEVEN." · "DARK BY HALF THREE." · "EIGHTEEN HOURS IN JUNE. SIX IN DECEMBER." · "THE TIDE TURNS EITHER WAY." Keep the client's three existing lines because they are already printed; do not add more of them.

cliches.item: "WE KEEP TIME. WE DON'T SELL IT." — a fortune cookie, and the brand explaining itself to itself on its own About page.
cliches.replace_with: Cut. If the About page needs an opening line, use a fact: "Started 2026, on a peninsula with sea on both sides."

cliches.item: "in the colour of sand at first light" · "the colour of the firth mid-afternoon" — poetic colour-as-place writing that directly breaks §1.2 ("Say what the thing is, what it is made of … **Specification is the persuasion**") one page after stating it.
cliches.replace_with: "380gsm loopback. Cream. Dyed after it was made, so no two match." Let the hour name carry the place — that is what the naming system is for. The description does not need to do it twice.

cliches.item: "IT WILL FADE. THAT IS THE POINT." / "IT FADES BECAUSE YOU WORE IT." — the standard garment-dye line of the last decade, used in three places, and the second sentence is the brand congratulating itself on the first.
cliches.replace_with: "IT WILL FADE." on the care label, full stop. Then the useful version on the product page, which Commercial already wrote: "Most shrinkage has already happened in the dye bath; expect up to a further 3% in length after the first wash."

cliches.item: THE LEDGER · THE MECHANISM · THE SETTLED FRAME · THE CORE · THE DROPS — five definite-article capitalised proper nouns for a website, an animation, a still image, four SKUs and three release dates. Capitalising a thing is not the same as designing it, and THE LEDGER is capitalised in four sections without ever being specified in one.
cliches.replace_with: Name one. "The Ledger" earns it if the website section ever gets written. Call the animation "the mechanism" in lower case, call the still "frame zero", and call the core and the drops what they are — always-on and drops.

cliches.item: The "that is not X, it is Y" antithesis, used 30+ times: "That is not a print error, it is a governance error" · "That discipline is not admin — it *is* the brand" · "That is not a metaphor about time" · "It is not a coincidence to be admired, it is a rule to be enforced" · "a brand system rather than a set of assets". It is the most recognisable machine-written cadence in the document.
cliches.replace_with: Delete the first half every time. "A printer printed what they were sent. Fix the files." Reads as written by a person who has seen it happen.

cliches.section: strategy §7 preamble, commercial preamble, verbal §6.3, visual §3.0
cliches.item: Self-important signposting: "The most useful page here. Print it and keep it where decisions get made." · "Read this one twice." · "**The single most important sentence in this entire document**" · "Section 2 is the most valuable page in this book." Four sections each claim to be the most important.
cliches.replace_with: Delete all four. A brand book that has to tell the reader which page matters has a structure problem, not an emphasis problem — put the three genuinely blocking decisions on one front page and let the rest be reference.

cliches.item: "A price is a promise."
cliches.replace_with: The spec it implies, which is already in the next sentence: "At £50 the tee is 240gsm or more, boxy, with a collar rib that survives washing. If the blank can't do that, the price is wrong."

cliches.item: "Stop watching: followers, impressions, reach, likes, 'engagement'. None of them have ever paid a printer." and "The list is the business. Followers are not." Two versions of the same line, both applause-seeking.
cliches.replace_with: "The weekly update is the eight numbers above. Nothing else goes in it."

cliches.item: "A Highland-Scottish streetwear label is one of approximately none" echoing "is one of roughly none" — a rhetorical flourish standing in for a search, repeated so it sounds established.
cliches.replace_with: "I could not find a contemporary streetwear label based in rural Highland Scotland. That is not the same as there not being one — check before printing the claim on anything."

cliches.item: "honest" and "honestly" as a virtue signal — "argued honestly", "the honest answers", "THE HONEST HEADLINE", "Honest positioning", "honest, not staged". Roughly twenty instances. Claiming honesty is what copy does when it has not yet shown a number.
cliches.replace_with: Remove the word and leave the evidence. "Compostable mailers cost 8.4–12.7p and most UK councils will not take them" is honest without saying so.

cliches.item: "The part worth stealing that nobody talks about."
cliches.replace_with: "Hanshaw's cogs ended up on the era's merchandise. That is the test for ours: if the mechanism can't be printed, it isn't the brand's."

gaps: **There is no website section, and the website was the original ask.** "THE LEDGER" is referenced as settled in Strategy, Verbal, Visual, Motion and Applications — the 404 spec, the QR destination (`ourtime.[tld]/ledger/[drop-code]`), the section-transition tick rule and the Instagram bio link all depend on it — and it is specified nowhere. No sitemap, no PDP layout, no navigation, no checkout, no mobile behaviour, no what-the-index-actually-is. The brand book builds the motion system for a site that has no structure.

**The domain and the handle are never decided, and they block the print run.** `OURTIME.[TLD]` and `@[handle]` appear as placeholders on the swing tag, the thank-you card, the lookbook back cover, the Instagram bio and every email footer. Commercial establishes that `ourtime.com` and `ourtime.co.uk` belong to a Match Group dating service and that the phrase is unsearchable, then says "pick something searchable" without picking it. Tags, labels and cards get ordered in weeks 6–7 of the launch plan; this decision has to be made in week 0.

**Nobody owns the brand book.** Visual specifies a master artwork library with "one owner, read-only to everyone else" and never names them, the book itself has no version number, no date of record, no change log and no process for adding a rule — and the document's entire argument is that OVERTIME happened because "there were several versions of the truth and no one had said which was the real one." It reproduces the exact failure it diagnoses. Needs: a version number on page one, a named owner, and a rule that a change to a locked value (hex, tracking, spelling, coordinates, hour) requires a new version and a re-issued supplier fact sheet.

**Three different pre-press checklists exist and none supersedes the others.** Visual §3.0.5 (six items), Verbal §6.3 (four items), Applications' "Checklist before any supplier is contacted" (ten items). They overlap, conflict in detail, and a founder at 4pm on a Friday will use whichever one he opens. One checklist, one page, one location.

**TikTok is named as the primary discovery channel and then never specified.** Strategy: "TikTok first, Instagram second, and a friend third — brand discovery for this group is almost entirely social and peer-validated." Applications specifies Instagram in detail and TikTok not at all. No format, no cadence, no what-a-TikTok-is-for, no relationship to the Reels spec.

**No customer-service voice.** The book governs product names, email subjects, care labels and 404s, but not the messages the founder will actually send most: the where-is-my-order DM, the wrong-size reply, the it-arrived-damaged reply, the "is this real" comment. Verbal's ban on exclamation marks explicitly extends "to a reply to a customer", which means there is a rule and no guidance. Needs six worked replies.

**No line on what happens when an OVERTIME garment surfaces.** Strategy recommends giving the misprints "to friends and family as unphotographed team stock" — which puts wrongly-printed garments into the world on people who will be photographed in them. There is no agreed sentence for when someone posts one, asks about one, or resells one.

**No wholesale or stockist position, and the pricing has silently decided it.** At 2.0–2.67× landed cost, a 50% wholesale margin is impossible on every piece in the range, so the book has ruled out stockists without saying so — while Strategy's Level 3 proposes "a physical presence or stockist in Inverness" and Audience notes the brand needs local backing. Either state "DTC only for two years, and here is why" or reprice for a keystone.

**No total launch budget.** Commercial costs the stock buy (≈£10,800) and nothing else. Missing and all imminent: photography, the website build, trade mark (£205+ plus attorney), insurance (£150–600), woven labels (500 MOQ), care labels, swing tags and string, mailers, tissue, stickers, cards, the typeface licence (£450–800 or £0), Shopify, and the strike-offs the print section requires. That is plausibly another £2,500–4,000 before a single sale, and the launch plan's gate is "you have the full cost of the buy in the bank plus 20% contingency" — which is the wrong number.

**The fit/gender question is never answered.** The audience is "majority male", the range is oversized unisex by implication, the size run is S–XXL — and no section says whether women are a stated customer, whether the size guide addresses them, or whether "oversized" is being sold as unisex. On an oversized range this is the single biggest returns variable after measurements.

**No image rights or model release process.** Visual mandates "Real people, not agency models" and Applications plans seeding to "people who will genuinely wear them and be seen". There is no release form, no usage term, no rule about what happens when someone asks to be removed, and no policy on reposting customer photos — which is the brand's main content source in year one.

**No claims policy for provenance and sustainability.** The book correctly warns against "Made in Scotland" without manufacture and against the word "compostable" under CMA Green Claims — then leaves "MADE IN [COUNTRY]" as a placeholder on the care label and says nothing about what may be claimed about the blanks, the dyehouse, the cotton or the word "recycled". The stated market is "premium and sustainable"; this will be asked in the first week.

**No drop-naming system, though colours get a locked ledger.** Drops appear as `[DROP NAME]` and "THE FIRST HOURS" with no rule for how the next one is named — the exact judgement call the hour-index was built to remove for colours. Three drops a year for five years is fifteen names an inexperienced founder has to invent under deadline.

**No accessibility policy outside the motion and contrast sections.** Nothing on alt text (the wordmark image in email is specified with alt text once, by accident), keyboard operation, focus states, plain-text email fallback, or the size-guide table's screen-reader behaviour. The contrast work is the best in the book; it stops at colour.

**No decision rule for what happens if drop one under-performs.** Commercial's sell-through targets and the strategy's falsification test ("if the units that actually sell are the loud graphic back-prints … then the brand is a graphics label") are both stated, and neither says what the founder does about it. Needs: at 90 days, if X then Y — a named threshold, a named response, and who decides.
unsupported_claims: "a founder who is from there" and "Nobody else can print 57.5878° N, 4.2383° W and mean it" (Strategy §1). Nothing in the brief establishes that the client has any connection to the Black Isle — the coordinates were changed from a generator's Chicago artefact three weeks ago. Applications §5.1 contradicts the assertion directly: "the brand should not claim the Black Isle unless there is a real connection to it … If he does not, the coordinates are a second fabrication." The book's largest strategic bet rests on an unverified biographical fact stated as established.

"UK streetwear in 2026 is a roughly £8.6bn market growing ~4.9% year on year" (Strategy §3), sourced to a single commercial report vendor, and used to support the further claim that "the growth has shifted from explosive to premium and sustainable" — which is an interpretation of that one source, not a finding from it.

"Finisterre … turning over roughly £24m by 2023" (Strategy §3), sourced to Wikipedia and a magazine feature. It is the load-bearing proof for the entire place-brand argument and deserves a filed-accounts figure, not an encyclopaedia entry.

"**Nobody is doing contemporary, premium, washed streetwear from rural/coastal Highland Scotland.**" (Strategy §3, repeated in Applications §5.1). No search method, date or scope is given for an absence claim that justifies the whole positioning.

"He has £60–£120 of genuinely discretionary clothing money a month and he spends it in concentrated bursts" (Strategy §4). Presented as audience fact with no source; it also underwrites the price bands.

"Corteiz's Royale heavyweight tee retails around $63–85 ([StockX])" (Strategy §4). StockX is a resale marketplace — that is a secondary-market range, not a retail price, and it is being used to set OUR TIME's tee price.

"Cole Buxton hoodies are £175" (Strategy §4 and §5) against Commercial §1.1's "£139 hoodie / £159 zip hoodie" and its cited Flannels range of £98–£175, from the same brand in the same month. One of the two comparison sets is wrong, and both are used to justify price.

The AS Colour Heavy Faded Tee 5082 at "**£16.25** (inferred from the 62.5% ratio)" (Commercial §1.2). The hero garment's blank cost — and therefore every margin, multiple and contribution figure in the book, plus the £8,956 drop-one total quoted to the pound — is an inference from five other styles. It is flagged, then used as if verified.

Whether AS Colour's published prices are ex-VAT is listed as UNVERIFIED, yet every landed cost and margin is computed as though they are. If they are inc-VAT the entire cost table is 20% optimistic on top of the separately-flagged irrecoverable-VAT point.

"Trims and packaging … realistically **£1.40–£1.85 per unit**" (Commercial §1.2) and "Relabelling labour … typically 50p–£1.00/unit" (Applications §1.1). Both flagged unverified; both are inside the landed costs that produce the book's headline margin rule.

"Outbound postage (Royal Mail Tracked 48, small parcel, online) −£5.25" (Commercial §1.5). The same section later warns that "fleece pieces may exceed small-parcel dimensions — weigh and measure a packed hoodie before you set your shipping rates." The contribution model that decides the entire paid-acquisition policy uses the rate the book says may not apply.

UK IPO fees "**£205 for the first class, £60 per additional class**" and "the first trade mark fee rise since 1998" (Commercial §7.1), stated flatly without an UNVERIFIED marker. The second clause in particular reads like a confident recollection rather than a checked fact.

"Plastic Packaging Tax: £228.82 per tonne from 1 April 2026" and the EPR thresholds "£2m turnover AND over 50 tonnes" (Applications §3.2), presented as settled compliance facts. The conclusions drawn from them are almost certainly right; the figures should carry the same UNVERIFIED discipline applied to print quotes.

"68% of Gen Z workers say they'd take a pay cut for better work-life balance, and 42% have turned down promotions" (Strategy §7.4), sourced to a content aggregator rather than the underlying survey, and used to argue a cultural direction of travel.

"nine hours of usable winter daylight" (Visual §3.4.3) against the brand's own headline figure of 6h41m (Strategy §3) and Visual's own "sun up around 09:00 and down around 15:30" (§3.5.3). One of the brand's two quantitative claims about itself is wrong in the section that governs the artwork carrying it.

"In idle mode … roughly **0.4% CPU**, against **6–9%** for the same complexity at 60 fps" (Motion §6.4). No device, no measurement, no method. The same section correctly instructs the developer to instrument and log p95 — which is an admission that the quoted figures were not.

Screen-print and embroidery minimums ("0.71mm positive, 1.06mm reverse", "1.5mm satin minimum") are trade-blog sourced and then written into a paragraph the founder is told to send to suppliers verbatim. Fine as a working rule, but it is presented to a printer as a specification, and one printer disagreeing with it will undermine the whole fact sheet.

The stem-width calculation behind Failure 1 — "A light-weight sans typically has stem widths around 5–7% of cap height … stems land at roughly 0.3–0.4mm" — is self-flagged as a rule of thumb, yet it is the sole basis for the 120mm wordmark minimum, which in turn contradicts Visual's 40mm. Measure the actual outlines once and the contradiction resolves itself.

No trade mark search has been run. Commercial admits it ("UNVERIFIED — I have not been able to confirm from the registers whether Overtime Sports holds UK or EU marks in class 25") while the rest of the book proceeds as though OUR TIME in class 25 is available and prints it on labels, tags, packaging, a lookbook and a domain.
strongest:
**The 24-hour colour index (Verbal §4.2–4.3): every colour is permanently assigned the hour it looks like on the Black Isle, and the product name is that hour plus the garment type.** It is the only idea in the book that does four jobs at once, and the only one built for the actual person who has to use it. It is a naming system (`0600 CREW`, `1200 TEE / GLOBE`), a merchandising plan the founder never has to write (\"Because the hour belongs to the colour, not the garment, a shared hour makes a set … 'The 0300 set' sells itself\"), a governance fix (the ledger is where a colour is born, with a hex beside it, which is exactly the single-source-of-truth discipline the OVERTIME failure demands), and a place story carried in a field that also has to exist anyway — the hours are a clock, the reason each colour holds its hour is Highland light.

The reason it is the best idea rather than merely the cleverest is the line \"**Naming becomes lookup, not judgement**.\" The brief says the client is non-technical and inexperienced at brand. Almost everything else in this book asks him to exercise taste under deadline; this asks him to read a row in a table. It also fails safe in the one direction the brand is most at risk from — Verbal's own rejected alternatives show the work, and \"numbers do not emote\" is the correct reason to prefer an index over Gloaming and Simmer Dim. And it scales past the founder: 168 slots, half-hours in reserve, one hour held back for the anniversary piece, and an explicit instruction that adding a colour means adding a row and touching nothing else.

Two repairs before it ships, both small: `0300` is currently assigned to two different colours (washed black `#171717` and washed black denim), which breaks the ledger's own no-reuse rule on the page that states it; and the emotional register of the early hours — `0300` \"the dead hour\", `0600` \"The hour you get up, not the hour you're due\" — is drifting back toward the pre-dawn grind vocabulary Strategy §7.4 bans. Name the hours after the light, not after the discipline, and the system is unimprovable.
weakest:
**The Black Isle strategy, because it is built on a fact nobody has checked.** Strategy §1 asserts \"a founder who is from there\" and \"Nobody else can print 57.5878° N, 4.2383° W and mean it\", and everything downstream presupposes it: the solstice-and-equinox release calendar, the whole of Visual §3.5.3 (approved locations, shoot windows, the grade), the 30%-location Instagram ratio, the lookbook sequence (place before product, twice), a third of the tagline bank, the welcome email, the swing tag, the thank-you card, the neck label and the compass star in the motion system. Applications §5.1 then quietly contradicts the premise — \"the brand should not claim the Black Isle unless there is a real connection to it … If he does not, the coordinates are a second fabrication and should be dropped rather than defended\" — and that paragraph is right. A label that has already shipped the wrong word on a garment cannot survive a second untrue thing on a garment, and coordinates are the most checkable claim a brand can print.

The risk is not that the strategy is bad. Given a real tie, it is the correct call and the book argues it well. The risk is that five sections of specification were written on top of an unverified input, so if the answer is no, this is not a dial-down — it is a rewrite of the photography direction, the release model, the copy architecture and the artwork on the hero tee.

**The fix, in order.** (1) Ask the cousin one question this week, in writing, before another penny is committed: *what is your actual connection to the Black Isle, and would you say it out loud in a shop without flinching?* Strategy already drafted that test and then failed to gate anything behind it — make it a gate. (2) Delete \"a founder who is from there\" and replace it with whatever is verifiably true, which may only be \"this is where the company is\" — Strategy §3's own answer, \"don't claim heritage — claim address\", is the honest floor and it is enough for Level 1. (3) If the answer is no, do not fall back to placelessness, which is the one outcome the book proves is fatal; fall back to the place that *is* true — where he lives, where the stock is packed, where the photographs can actually be taken — and apply the identical rigour. (4) Whatever the answer, add the coordinates and the two daylight figures to the protected-values list beside the spelling, so that the number on the globe tee can never again be something a tool generated.

Runner-up, and worth saying: Motion is eight pages of canvas engineering — DPR capping, offscreen sprites, escapement easing, an ffmpeg export path — for a brand that does not yet have a website, a photograph of most of its range, or a printer who has agreed a minimum line weight. The Mechanism is genuinely good work, but it is specified at a level of detail the rest of the book has not earned, and its central claim (that it is the same object as the printed dial) is not true as drafted. Build the settled frame first, ship it as the still, and hold the animation until there is a site to put it on.

contradictions.issue: Strategy prescribes a "Recommended launch cut: ~14 SKUs" and lists 14 colourways including two polos, two shorts, the sweatpant and the washed-black jean. Commercial §2.2 prescribes "Three garment types. Six colourways. 320 units" and explicitly cuts polos, shorts and jeans. Strategy is the section a founder reads first and it authorises roughly double the buy Commercial says he can survive.
contradictions.resolution: Delete the list in Strategy §7.20 and replace it with a pointer: "The launch range is decided in Commercial §2.2. Nothing else is made." Also fix the word "SKU" — Strategy's 14 items are 14 colourways = 70 SKUs at S–XXL, which is the number that actually gets ordered.

contradictions.between: Verbal §6.1 vs Visual §3.1.6 vs Applications §0.2 vs Motion §4.3
contradictions.issue: The word-space rule — the single rule that exists because garments shipped misprinted — is specified four different ways. Verbal: tracking 0.40em, word gap ≥1.0em, "never less than 2.5× the gap between two letters", CSS 0.40/0.60. Visual: tracking +0.32em, word gap +0.96em, "≥ 3.0×", CSS 0.32/0.64. Applications: "3× the letter tracking value". Motion: "word gap baked in at a fixed 0.62em" with letterspacing animating 0.38em→0.32em. Verbal's own numbers (0.40 + 0.60 = 1.0em = 2.5×) violate the 3× rule the other three sections state.
contradictions.resolution: Pick one pair of numbers, put them in one place, and have every other section cite it rather than restate it. Visual's 0.32em / 0.64em (= 0.96em total, exactly 3.0×) is the internally consistent set. Then delete the numbers from Verbal, Applications and Motion and replace with "see Visual §3.1.6".

contradictions.issue: Same object, opposite spec. Verbal: "**Front:** the lockup only. OT monogram above, OUR TIME wordmark below, `EST. 2026` beneath." Applications: "**Face A (front)** — OT monogram, 26mm wide, centred… Nothing else. No tagline, no URL, no 'EST. 2026'." Applications sets the tag at 45 × 90mm / 450gsm; Visual §3.6.2 sets "Hang tag: 50 × 90 mm, 400 gsm uncoated".
contradictions.resolution: One swing-tag spec, in Applications, with the artwork and the die size. Delete Verbal §3.8 and Visual's hang-tag line. This is a printed object with a die charge — two specs means two dies.

contradictions.between: Strategy Pillar 1 / §7.10 vs Visual §3.2.1 vs Motion §2.3
contradictions.issue: Strategy states as an absolute: "No accent colour is ever introduced" and "**No accent colour.**" Visual §3.2.1 has a role headed "**Accent (the only one)** #54647E Washed Denim — links, active states, data marks, the coordinate line, the one thing on a page allowed to be a colour." Motion §2.3 makes #54647E the one saturated element in the Mechanism.
contradictions.resolution: Visual and Motion are right and Strategy is over-written. Change Strategy to "No accent beyond #54647E, and no colour above C* 20" so the rule matches the system that already exists.

contradictions.issue: Verbal merchandises "**THE 2200 SET** — navy. Two tees, polo, crew, hoodie, short." But the 2200 SHORT is #141925 and the tops are #141B2C, and Visual Rule 3.2.2a says the two navies "may **never appear in the same photograph, flat-lay set, or product grid**." The set the naming system generates is banned by the colour system.
contradictions.resolution: Resolve the navy first (Visual open item 2), then the set is legal. Until it is resolved, add a line to Verbal §4.9: "The 2200 SET cannot be photographed or listed as a set until one navy is chosen."

contradictions.issue: Verbal's own rule: "A colour's hour is assigned once and never changes… never reuse or reassign one." It then assigns Washed Black #171717 to 0300 and also assigns "Washed Black Denim *measure*" — a different, unmeasured colour on a different fibre — to 0300 (`OT-0300-JEAN-PAT`). §4.9 then sells "THE 0300 SET — washed black… Six pieces, head to toe, one colour" when the jean is demonstrably not that colour.
contradictions.resolution: Give the denim its own free hour (0200 is open) and rewrite the 0300 set as five pieces. The same fault is latent in Cream (#CFC2B4 claimed across jersey, fleece and shorting) and White (#FAF6F6 claimed across jersey and piqué) — the two-navies lesson was never applied to the other colours.

contradictions.issue: Verbal fixes the CTA vocabulary — "`SEE THE INDEX` · `VIEW THE DROP` · `BUY` · `SET A REMINDER`. Never `SHOP NOW`." Applications' drop email specifies "`SHOP NOW →` button, above the fold" and repeats it in the back-in-stock email.
contradictions.resolution: Change the Applications buttons to `VIEW THE DROP` and `BUY`. Trivial, but it is exactly the kind of thing that ships because two documents disagreed.

contradictions.issue: Verbal's drop-announcement template ends "Nothing here is restocked." Commercial's model is "**THE CORE** — Tee (navy, white), zip hoodie (navy, cream) — Availability: Always on, **restocked**." Drop one under Commercial §2.2 is entirely core pieces, so the template as written would be a false statement on the launch email.
contradictions.resolution: Split the template: one announcement format for THE CORE ("Restocked" / "Always on") and one for THE DROPS ("Run of 120. Not restocked."). Verbal currently only has the second.

contradictions.issue: Three different care instructions for the same garment. Verbal: "HANG DRY." Applications' literal label block: "TUMBLE DRY LOW". Commercial's mandatory product-page disclosure: "**Wash cold, inside out. Hang dry. Do not tumble dry.**" A physical label saying tumble dry low, on a garment whose product page says do not tumble dry, is a shrinkage argument the brand loses.
contradictions.resolution: Settle on "DO NOT TUMBLE DRY" (correct for garment-dyed heavyweight cotton) and make the label, the swing tag, the product page and the thank-you card carry identical wording. Put that wording in one place and have the other three cite it.

contradictions.issue: Commercial correctly says "**Do not write:** 'no returns on sale items', 'no returns without original packaging'… all four are unenforceable." Verbal's order-confirmation template then writes "Wrong size, wrong colour, wrong decision: 30 days, unworn, tags on." Under the Consumer Contracts Regulations the 14-day cancellation right cannot be conditioned on tags being attached — you may only deduct for diminished value.
contradictions.resolution: Change the line to: "Changed your mind? 30 days. We only ask you handle it the way you would in a shop. Reply to this email and we'll sort it." Keep tags language out of any customer-facing text.

contradictions.between: Visual §3.2.3 / open item 4 vs Applications §4.2 vs Commercial §1.2
contradictions.issue: Visual sets the default print method as "**water-based / discharge**" and makes a white-on-navy discharge strike-off a blocking open item. Applications §4.2 then shows discharge "only works on reactive-dyed cotton" and that garment-dyed and pigment-dyed fabric "resist discharge activation". Commercial then picks AS Colour *Heavy Faded* / *Relax Faded* blanks — precisely the garment-dyed case where discharge fails.
contradictions.resolution: Delete discharge as the default. State in Visual: "Default is soft-hand water-based screen print. Discharge is available only if the blank is confirmed reactive-dyed in writing." Visual's open item 4 then becomes "get a water-based white-on-navy strike-off", which is the test actually needed.

contradictions.issue: Visual permanently assigns navy and washed black to the **PAPER** ground #DFDDDE — "in photography, on the website, in the lookbook, on packaging, in a paid ad." Applications' lookbook spec says pp. 6–13 are "full-garment flat-lay (dead-on, soft top light, **#0F0F0F ground**)" for the whole range, and the Instagram direction says "near-black ground" throughout. Four of the six drop-one pieces are navy or washed black, so the launch shoot as specified in Applications is forbidden by Visual and would produce a 1.12:1 silhouette.
contradictions.resolution: Add one line to Applications §5.2 and §6.3: "Ground per Visual §3.2.5 — dark garments shoot on #DFDDDE." And warn the founder explicitly that his launch grid will be mostly paper-ground, which is correct and will look wrong to him.

contradictions.issue: Verbal puts the hour code "on the internal neck label, under the wordmark, small." Applications §1.2 rules the neck label is "**OT monogram only.** Not the wordmark" — because thread cannot hold the wordmark's hairlines — and §1.4 puts the size on the care label. There is no wordmark on the neck label to sit under, so Verbal's placement is unbuildable.
contradictions.resolution: Applications wins on manufacturing grounds. Move the hour code to the printed care label, set as the line under the size band — it is printed, not woven, so a four-digit number at 6pt is trivial. Rewrite Verbal §4.2 accordingly.

contradictions.between: Strategy §2 vs Visual open item 6 vs Commercial §7.2
contradictions.issue: The OVERTIME garments get three rulings. Strategy: "never sold, never photographed, never listed, and never turned into a cute 'misprint drop' story." Commercial: "Do not sell them. Not at a discount, not as seconds, not quietly." Visual open item 6: "Recall/relabel or **sell through** the existing OVERTIME garments as a deliberate, named first-run anomaly — decide which." Visual reopens the exact door the other two nailed shut.
contradictions.resolution: Delete Visual open item 6. Two sections already made the call and it is the right one — and if Overtime Sports holds a UK class 25 mark, even giving them away is distribution. Destroy them and record the write-off.

contradictions.between: Visual §3.1.4 vs Applications §4.5 Failure 1 vs Motion §4.3
contradictions.issue: Wordmark minimum size is given four ways: 32mm litho and 40mm screen/DTG on fabric and 128px screen (Visual), "minimum reproduction width of 120mm on garment" (Applications), and 132px web / 180px video (Motion). The 40mm vs 120mm gap is 3× and decides whether the wordmark can appear on a chest, a shorts leg or a small tag at all.
contradictions.resolution: Measure the actual outlines and print a test sheet at 20/25/32/40/60/120mm on the real blank. Then write one number per process into Visual §3.1.4 and have Applications and Motion cite it. Until that test exists, hold Applications' conservative 120mm, because it is the only one that assumes washed heavyweight cotton.

contradictions.issue: Visual specifies tethered capture, f/8–f/11, 50–85mm, a 120cm octabox, 5200K fixed with the grey-card shot kept, a rig levelled to 90° ± 0.5°, and a physical matte plaster ground at LRV ≈3% and sheen ≤5 GU. Applications §5 opens: "Written for one person posting alone, with a job, with no photographer on retainer. **Everything below is achievable on a phone.**" Both cannot be true of the same flat-lays.
contradictions.resolution: State the tiering explicitly: phone and window light for Instagram texture and process; the rig spec for the ~12 product shots that go on the PDP. Then give the £150 version of the rig — levelled tripod, one bounced source, painted MDF board — so the spec is actually reachable.

contradictions.issue: Three price lists. Crew: £85–95 (Strategy) / £75 (Commercial) / £85 in Verbal's order-confirmation example. Zip hoodie: £95–110 (Strategy) / £85 (Commercial). Strategy argues "the ~£100 hoodie is the band where 'this is better than you expected' is a repeatable experience"; Commercial argues anything above £85 "is a bet on a reputation that does not exist yet."
contradictions.resolution: Commercial's list wins because it is the only one derived from landed cost. Delete the bands from Strategy §4 and replace with a pointer. Fix Verbal's £85 crew to £75.

contradictions.issue: Strategy builds the entire Black Isle argument on a measured swing of "18 hours 7 minutes" and "6 hours 41 minutes", and Applications and Verbal both use the ~6.5 hour figure. Visual §3.4.3 writes "**nine hours of usable winter daylight**" in the same book.
contradictions.resolution: Change Visual to "six and a half hours of winter daylight". This figure is going on a website and possibly on a garment; it must be one number, and it must be the correct one.

contradictions.issue: "No always-on countdown timer" is stated absolutely in three sections and Motion bans "Any countdown, drop timer, or 'scarcity' clock" outright. Applications then permits "A countdown Story sticker on the 24 hours before an actual drop" and Commercial permits a truthful units-remaining counter.
contradictions.resolution: The nuance is right but the rule is written as an absolute, so the founder will either break it or over-obey it. Restate it once, everywhere: "No timer that resets. A real, finite deadline or a true remaining-units count is permitted. A perpetual countdown is not."

contradictions.between: Verbal §3.3 fit lines vs Commercial §1.2 blank choice
contradictions.issue: Verbal's worked examples state "380gsm loopback cotton", "240gsm piqué cotton", "14oz rigid denim" and "320gsm cotton". The blanks Commercial actually costs are a 320gsm hood, zip hood, shorts and joggers and a 220gsm Chad polo. A founder will paste those example lines straight onto a product page.
contradictions.resolution: Strip every gsm from the Verbal examples and replace with `[GSM]`, keeping the standing rule Verbal already has: "if you do not know the gsm, ask the factory before you write the line." A stated weight is a product claim he can be held to.

cliches.item: The "X is not Y, it is Z" construction, used dozens of times: "That discipline is not admin… it *is* the brand"; "It is not a coincidence to be admired, it is a rule to be enforced"; "That is not a metaphor about time. That is a place where…"; "A number is the brand; an adjective is every other brand"; "the time theme is the *expression*; the Black Isle is the *asset*"; "That is a brand system rather than a set of assets"; "A launch to nobody is not a launch; it is an expensive photograph."
cliches.replace_with: Keep three of them, at the three moments that actually matter, and rewrite the rest as plain statements. This construction is the loudest single tell that the book was drafted by a machine, and its force decays to zero by the fourth use.

cliches.item: "Scarcity that's always on isn't scarcity, it's a Shopify app" — reproduced near-verbatim four times across four sections.
cliches.replace_with: State it once, in Commercial §4.2 where the drop model is decided. Everywhere else: "No perpetual countdown (see Commercial §4.2)." It was a good line once.

cliches.item: "The single most…" / "the single biggest…" as an intensifier — more than twenty occurrences: single most important sentence, single highest-leverage decision, single biggest driver of returns, single cheapest thing to get wrong, single most likely production disappointment, single most-built cliché, single greatest safety feature, single best list-growth mechanism.
cliches.replace_with: Cut it everywhere except two places. When eight things are the single most important thing, the founder cannot triage — and triage is the one job this book has.

cliches.item: "made for people in the unwatched middle of building something" — and the whole 48-word sentence it sits inside.
cliches.replace_with: Something the cousin can say out loud in a shop without wincing: "Heavyweight, garment-dyed clothing from the Black Isle. Made to be worn every day and to look better for it." Test any positioning line by whether a 22-year-old would say it to a stranger.

cliches.item: "A slogan is not a moat." / "Specificity is what travels; genericism is what stays home." / "be from somewhere, be *for* everyone" / "Nobody in Tokyo cares about Queens either." Aphorisms shaped like insight, none falsifiable, all familiar from a hundred brand decks.
cliches.replace_with: Delete them. The Finisterre and Aimé Leon Dore evidence already in the section does the work; the aphorisms are what you write when you do not trust your own evidence.

cliches.item: "NOBODY HANDS YOU THE HOUR." · "NO ONE CLOCKS YOU IN." · "SECONDS ARE CHEAP. HOURS AREN'T." · "SET YOUR OWN HOUR." — the exact register of the grind-culture apparel that §1.3 spends a page banning. "SECONDS ARE CHEAP. HOURS AREN'T." is a gym caption with a clock in it.
cliches.replace_with: Keep only the place lines, which are the ones nobody else can write: `LONG DAYS. SHORT WINTERS.` · `FIRST LIGHT TO LAST.` · `LIGHT PERMITTING.` · `THE WEATHER DOESN'T ASK.` · `IT FADES BECAUSE YOU WORE IT.` Cut the rest. Twenty-one taglines is nineteen too many for a six-piece launch.

cliches.item: "WE KEEP TIME. WE DON'T SELL IT." — an agency line about the brand, addressed to nobody, that only lands if you have read the brand book.
cliches.replace_with: Cut it. If a line needs the About page to make sense, it is not a line, it is a footnote.

cliches.item: "Empty space is what says the brand isn't worried."
cliches.replace_with: "Leave the page empty. Filling it is what makes it look cheap." The rule itself is one of the best things in the book; the epigram undercuts it.

cliches.section: Commercial §5, end of the launch plan
cliches.item: "Making that call in advance, on a date, is the difference between a founder and someone who is hoping." — motivational-poster register, in a book with a hard ban on motivational register.
cliches.replace_with: "Put 4 November in the calendar now, and decide on that day, on whatever evidence you have then."

cliches.item: "WIND IT. WEAR IT." — annotated in the book itself as "the closest to a joke we allow", which is the tell. It is a watch-shop line.
cliches.replace_with: Cut. A brand that has to annotate its own joke does not have one.

cliches.item: "Everything in this price bracket looks like it came from nowhere. Ours came from somewhere, and we can prove it." The "and we can prove it" tag is stock pitch-deck cadence.
cliches.replace_with: "Nothing else at this price is from anywhere. This is."

cliches.item: "premium-minimal", "quiet luxury adjacent", "the quiet voice / the loud voice", "vintage-athletic" used as if self-defining. "Premium" appears roughly forty times in a book whose own Verbal §1.2 bans it: "No 'premium' in customer-facing copy."
cliches.replace_with: Internal documents may use it, but define it once against something measurable — weight, wash, one mark, no gloss, no accent — and then use the measurable version. Otherwise it is exactly the adjective the book warns about, applied to itself.

cliches.item: "People buy from small brands because they can see the smallness." and "early-stage brands need a hundred people who care, not a hundred thousand who scroll past" — two lightly-reworded versions of the 1,000-true-fans platitude, in two different sections.
cliches.replace_with: Keep one, cut the other. They are the same thought and the repetition makes both look borrowed.

cliches.item: "Their sequence is a *journey through* a mechanism. Ours is a *mechanism, observed*." plus "one object, built once, used everywhere" plus "That constraint is the whole point."
cliches.replace_with: The take/leave table underneath already says all of this concretely and better. Cut the three framings above it and open the section with the table.

cliches.section: Applications §0 and Visual §3.0 and Commercial §5 Week 0
cliches.item: The OVERTIME misprint story is retold from scratch four times, each time as a revelation — "That is not a print error, it is a governance error" / "a *supply of truth* error" / "The brand has been running without one, and it has already cost you".
cliches.replace_with: Tell it once, at the front of the book, in three sentences. Then reference it. Retelling it in every section makes the founder's one mistake the loudest recurring character in his own brand book.

gaps: **Does the cousin actually have a tie to the Black Isle?** The entire Strategy section, the biggest motif, the coordinates on the tag, the neck label, the bio, the welcome email subject line and the lookbook's first three pages all depend on it. Applications §5.1 is the only place that raises it — "If he does not, the coordinates are a second fabrication and should be dropped" — and it is raised deep in a later section. Nobody has asked him, and nothing in the book blocks on the answer. This is question one of week zero, ahead of the trade mark search.

**Does a vector master of the logo actually exist?** Every section assumes outlined `.ai` artwork in a master folder. The coordinates were "a generator artefact", which strongly suggests the artwork is AI-generated raster. If so, none of this book is executable and the real week-zero job is paying a designer £300–£800 to redraw the monogram and wordmark as proper vectors with the shear angles measured and recorded. No section asks the question or budgets the answer.

**The domain is never chosen.** Commercial §7.1 establishes that `ourtime.com` and `ourtime.co.uk` belong to a Match Group dating service with 190,000 UK members, says "pick something searchable", and stops. Meanwhile `OURTIME.[TLD]` is printed as a placeholder on the swing tag, the thank-you card, the lookbook back cover and every email footer. Nothing can go to a printer until this is decided, and no section owns the decision.

**The Instagram handle is never chosen either.** "secure `@ourtime` or the closest clean variant" — @ourtime will not be available. No fallback convention is offered, and Commercial §7.1's advice ("pick one consistent, ownable string — the monogram plus a qualifier") never produces an actual string.

**There is no total launch budget.** Commercial gives £10,800 for stock and never adds trims and labels (500-unit woven MOQ, bought before the range is proven), samples, wash tests, four strike-offs at £100–200 each, insurance £150–600, trade mark £205+, Shopify ~£228/yr, domain, typefaces £0–800, photography, mailers, tags and string. The realistic all-in is £14,000–£18,000 and the founder is never told that number — nor where it comes from, nor what happens if drop one sells 40% instead of 65%.

**VAT on the sale price is missing from every margin figure.** §7.3 covers input VAT and mentions £8.33 in passing, but §1.3's table, §1.5's contribution and §6's metric targets all treat a £50 RRP as £50 of revenue. See the weakest-part note — this is the one that costs money.

**The chest mark is never specified.** Polo, crew and zip hoodie all carry "OT chest" embroidery and it is the mark on most of the range, but no section gives its width, its distance from the high point of shoulder, its distance from a placket, or a placement diagram. Visual says embroidery minimum 25mm; Applications assumes "a 60mm chest placement" without ever making it a rule. It is the first thing an embroiderer asks for.

**The fit block is asserted, not sourced.** Commercial §3.2 promises "One block, honestly described… the same body: dropped shoulder, boxy through the chest, short-to-square length, wide sleeve" across tee, crew and zip hoodie. If the blanks are AS Colour, the fit is AS Colour's across three different styles, and nobody has checked that 5082, 5160 and 5170 read as one body. Buy one of each and measure before that promise goes on a product page.

**Nobody decides which blank supplier.** Commercial says "AS Colour or equivalent" and prices off AS Colour; Applications' entire print ruling hangs on the dye method; no section names a supplier, a second source, or what to do if the answer to "reactive, pigment or garment-dyed?" is the wrong one. It is a checklist item with no decision rule attached, which means it will be answered by whoever replies to the email first.

**No wholesale or stockist economics.** Strategy Level 3 dangles "a physical presence or stockist in Inverness" and the competitive set implies a route through retail. At 2.01× on the tee there is no wholesale business at any volume — a 2.2× wholesale multiple would put the trade price below landed cost. Nobody names that ceiling, and it silently forecloses a route Strategy promises.

**The Mechanism has no phase-two ruling and no build cost.** Motion §8 asks for a hand-written Canvas 2D clockwork engine with a sampled bézier solver, OffscreenCanvas sprite caching, DPR capping, IntersectionObserver / battery / Save-Data gates, a fixed-step PNG export path and an ffmpeg pipeline — inside a Shopify theme, for a non-technical founder. That is several days of specialist front-end work and the single likeliest cause of a missed December launch. Motion §6.1's settled frame already does six of the seven jobs statically. No section says "ship the still; build the Mechanism after drop one."

**Nobody chooses the typeface.** Visual offers a ~£450–800 paid system and a £0 OFL system and leaves it as open item 3. It gates the lookbook, the site, the labels and every print file. Make the call in the book: take the OFL system at launch (Archivo Expanded Black Italic / Switzer / IBM Plex Mono), because the merchandise-licence trap Visual correctly identifies does not arise at all under OFL.

**Fulfilment is undefined.** Where does 320 units of stock live — a spare room, on a home insurance policy that Commercial §7.4 warns almost certainly excludes it? Who packs? What is the dispatch SLA when he is at work? Where do returns go — and if that is a home address, it is about to be published on a returns policy.

**No customer-service position.** There is a beautiful order-confirmation template and nothing at all for the first "it doesn't fit", "the colour is different from the photo" or "the print cracked" email — which, on a garment-dyed range with a 25–30% return rate, is the most-written copy of year one.

**The photography plan does not match the buy.** Visual §3.5.1 says "every one of the ~31 colourways gets one" flat-lay and specifies five crops from one master capture; the launch is six colourways. Nobody reconciles the two, budgets the shoot, or says who shoots on-body — which Visual §3.5.2 admits "does not exist yet" while Commercial's plan assumes on-body with stated model height and size in week 8.

**No stop condition.** Strategy offers a falsification test ("Watch the sell-through by SKU in the first two drops") but no section says what result triggers what action, what "the Black Isle bet failed" looks like in numbers, or at what point he stops buying stock. Commercial §6 gets closest — "When it exceeds what you can afford to lose, stop buying" — without ever asking him to write that figure down.

**The website — the original ask — is never specified.** "THE LEDGER" is invoked in four sections as an existing direction. No section lists the pages, decides Shopify theme vs headless, or explains how a custom Canvas intro coexists with a Shopify checkout and its session handling. The person building it has no handoff.

**No decision on how prices are displayed** (inc or ex VAT), no decision on international shipping, and no decision on whether the launch ships outside the UK — which matters, because post-Brexit EU sales pull in IOSS registration or customer-paid duty, and a £50 tee becomes a £70 experience and a return the brand pays for twice.

**Nothing on what fixing the navy actually costs.** Visual open item 2 says "Choose **one** navy and migrate." With bought-in blanks that may be impossible — the two navies are two suppliers' dye lots on two fabrics. Nobody says so, and the honest resolution is probably "we have two navies, they are never photographed together, and they are named differently", not a migration.

**The 24-hour index is built and then never used anywhere else.** Verbal §4 constructs a full naming system with SKUs (`OT-0600-CREW-XX-L`). Commercial's drop plan, Visual's file-naming convention (`TEE_NAVY_BACK_HOURGLASS_v4_APPROVED.pdf`) and Applications' swing tag all ignore it. Either adopt it across the book — file names, purchase orders, the shop, the care label — or cut it. A naming system used in one section is not a naming system.

**No launch-day operational plan.** Commercial §5 says "you can physically pack and post 40 orders across one weekend" and stops. Nothing on packing-station setup, label printing, when the Post Office actually accepts 40 parcels, what happens if 120 orders land, or who covers the day job.
unsupported_claims: **"He has £60–£120 of genuinely discretionary clothing money a month"** (Strategy §4). No source at all, and the entire £45–£85 price architecture stands on it. For 18–26 in the UK in 2026 this is optimistic for a large part of the segment. It needs either a source or a downgrade to "spends in £50–£100 bursts a few times a year" — which would change the drop cadence argument.

**"UK streetwear in 2026 is a roughly £8.6bn market growing ~4.9% year on year"** (Strategy §3) — one aggregator report, no methodology, no definition of what counts as streetwear. It is then used to support a much stronger claim ("the winners now win on story and make, not on hype velocity") that the cited figure does not contain.

**"68% of Gen Z workers say they'd take a pay cut for better work-life balance, and 42% have turned down promotions"** (Strategy §7.4) — cited to an aggregator rather than the underlying survey, and it measures employment preference, not apparel purchase behaviour. It is used to conclude that "hustle-porn is a receding cultural position" about a customer who is demonstrably still buying gym-motivation sweatshirts in volume.

**"£24m turnover by 2023" for Finisterre, and the inference that "remoteness was the asset, not the handicap"** (Strategy §3). The turnover figure is Wikipedia-sourced; the causal claim is a post-hoc story about a 20-year-old brand in a different category (technical surf) with a different route to market (wholesale plus own stores). It proves the strategy is possible, not that it is likely.

**The AS Colour 50+ price for the hero tee is inferred, not observed.** Commercial §1.2: "£16.25 (inferred from the 62.5% ratio)". Every margin figure, the £8,956 drop-one buy and the £10,800 cash requirement rest on it. Compounding that, the book also flags as unverified "whether AS Colour's displayed prices are ex-VAT" — if they are inclusive, the tee lands at ~£13.54 ex-VAT and every number in §1.3 moves. Two unresolved unknowns sit underneath the most load-bearing table in the book.

**"Royal Mail Tracked 48, small parcel, £5.25 online"** is used as *the* shipping cost, while the book itself notes "fleece pieces may exceed small-parcel dimensions". A packed 320gsm zip hoodie is almost certainly a medium parcel, which is roughly double — and the "free UK shipping at £75" threshold in §1.5 was set on the small-parcel figure. Weigh and measure a packed hoodie before that threshold is published anywhere.

**"UK fashion AOV was £91.53 in May 2026"** (Commercial §6, metric 4, target "≥ £90"). That index reports its own client base, which skews to established mid-market retailers. Setting a first-year target off it, on a range whose cheapest item is £45, is setting a target that cannot be hit until the hoodie outsells the tee.

**"UK online fashion returns run at roughly 30%… 56% of apparel sellers reporting 30%+"** — one trade-press article, and the 56% is sellers' self-reported perception, not measured returns. The directional point is sound; the precision is not, and §6 converts it into a pass/fail metric with a 25% threshold.

**"'Our time' is a common English phrase, which makes the words alone weak and hard to register or enforce"** (Commercial §7.1) — stated as settled law. Commonness is not the test; distinctiveness in relation to class 25 goods is, and short common phrases are registered for clothing routinely. The recommendation that follows — file the device only — would leave the *name* unprotected against anyone who later files the words, which is the more likely attack.

**The Overtime Sports risk is raised and then left open.** "`UNVERIFIED — I have not been able to confirm from the registers whether Overtime Sports holds UK or EU marks in class 25. Someone must check.`" This is the one unverified item in the book that can cost serious money, and it is unaddressed where it matters most: if that mark exists, the misprinted garments are potentially infringing articles, and "give them to friends and family as unphotographed team stock" is still distribution. Check UK IPO, EUIPO and WIPO, and destroy the garments either way.

**"Decorative matter making up 7% or less of the product is excluded — which is why a screen print does not need declaring"** (Applications §1.3). The 7% exemption concerns fibres in decorative matter, not prints and inks generally. The conclusion happens to be right; the stated reason is not, and a founder repeating the reason to a trading standards officer will not enjoy the conversation.

**The UKFT care-label licence cost** — "likely a low-hundreds annual figure for a micro-brand" — is a guess sitting inside a paragraph that concludes "**Practical route for launch: get the licence.**" The same section correctly notes the symbols are not legally mandatory. Launch with written care instructions and price the licence before deciding.

**The stem-width calculation in Applications §4.5 Failure 1** ("stems land at roughly 0.3–0.4mm") is explicitly a rule of thumb applied to a typeface nobody has measured, and it drives the book's most consequential artwork rule (wordmark ≥120mm on garment). Measure the actual outlines — the rule may be far too strict, or not strict enough.

**Two data points carry a category-level conclusion.** "Discipline.clothing" plus a single Amazon POD listing are offered as proof that "Nothing in that space is ownable" (Strategy §1) — the premise the whole pivot rests on. The conclusion is probably right; the evidence is thin enough that a sceptical founder can wave it away, and he will, because the grind copy is already printed on his garments.

**"GARMENT DYED IN SMALL RUNS" (Instagram bio) and "Garment-dyed in small lots, so no two run the same" (Verbal §3.2)** are factual claims about a dye process the brand does not perform and cannot observe, on blanks bought from a third party.
