Verbal's own §1.4 rule — "Never claim manufacture you do not have" — applies directly. Say "garment-dyed" (true of the blank) and drop "in small runs / small lots" unless the supplier confirms it in writing.

**"Below 32 mm / 128 px the gap is no longer reliably reproduced"** (Visual §3.1.6), and the whole minimum-size table, are presented as measured facts. They are reasonable estimates for a wordmark whose actual stroke weights have never been recorded. Print a test sheet at 20/25/32/40mm on the actual blank and record the real floor — a £0 test that converts four guesses into facts and directly protects the brand's one known failure mode.

**"Embroidery for a left-chest mark at 50+ runs around £3.75 per garment"** and the whole decoration price ladder are single-source, drawn from one workwear supplier's published guide. Workwear pricing and premium-streetwear finishing are different jobs with different minimums; the book's own instruction to "brief the digitiser explicitly to preserve the shear angles" is exactly the kind of request that moves a job out of the published rate.
strongest: **The 24-hour colour index (Verbal §4.2–4.3).** It is the only idea in the book that makes the founder *better* rather than merely constraining him. Every other system here is a rule he has to remember and obey; this one removes a decision he is guaranteed to get wrong. He picks a colour, the colour already owns an hour, the hour is in a locked table — "Naming becomes lookup, not judgement." It is derived from both halves of the brand at once (a clock, and the Highland light that gives each colour its hour), it scales to 168 slots before it strains, it cannot go twee because numbers do not emote, and — the part that earns its keep commercially — because the hour belongs to the colour rather than the garment, the range merchandises itself into sets with no merchandising plan: "Everything at 0300 is washed black, head to toe." Reserving 0000 for the annual anniversary piece is a genuinely elegant touch. It costs nothing, it is implementable this afternoon, and it is the one piece of intellectual property in this book that a competitor could not lift without visibly copying. Two fixes before it ships: resolve the 0300 collision (washed black and washed black denim cannot share an hour under the system's own rule), and then use it *everywhere* — file names, purchase orders, the shop, the care label — or it is decoration. Close runner-up: Visual §3.2.5's permanent ground assignment, which solves a real problem (a range that is over half dark garments being photographed on a near-black ground) with one rule and one number, and has the confidence to say the mixed grid that results "is *correct*, not broken."
weakest: **The price and margin architecture in Commercial §1.3–§1.5. It is not merely uncertain — it contains an omission that makes every number in it wrong in the same direction.** Every multiple and gross-margin figure treats the RRP as revenue: the tee at £50 returns "2.01× / 50%". But a UK retail price is VAT-inclusive, so once the brand registers, £50 is £41.67 of revenue and the multiple is 1.68× at about 40%. §7.3 half-spots this ("handing HMRC £8.33 unless you raise the price") and never feeds it back into the table, so the book simultaneously warns that costs are ×1.2 and forgets that revenue is ÷1.2. Even on the pre-registration numbers the hero product already fails the book's own rule ("roughly 2.5×–3× landed cost… At 2× you have a hobby"); post-registration so does the crew, and contribution on a single-tee order falls from £18.65 to roughly £10 before returns — against a stated CAC of £20–£45 the book already says he cannot afford. Layered on top: the tee's £16.25 blank cost is *inferred* from a ratio; the book flags as unverified whether AS Colour's published prices are even ex-VAT; and the drop-one buy costs both tees at £24.85, the two-print-position figure, on the same page where §1.4 tells him to use one position. The most load-bearing table in the book therefore rests on an inferred input, an unresolved tax question, an internal inconsistency and a structural omission. **The fix, in order:** (1) confirm whether AS Colour's displayed prices include VAT — one phone call, and it moves every number; (2) rebuild §1.3 with two columns, pre-registration and post-registration, so he can see the cliff coming rather than meeting it in month eleven; (3) accept that the tee cannot carry this brand and say so plainly — one print position, £55 not £50, and make the zip hoodie the hero of every page, every email and every campaign image, because at 2.67× it is the only thing in the range that pays him; (4) state the crossing answer now rather than deferring it: prices rise roughly 8–10% at registration, or margin goes. Get this wrong and he discovers it with £9,000 of stock in a spare room and no way to price out of it.

contradictions.between: Verbal §6.1–6.2 vs Visual §3.1.6/§3.3.4 vs Applications §0.2 vs Motion §4.3
contradictions.issue: The single rule the book exists to enforce — the OUR TIME word space — is specified four incompatible ways. Verbal: 'a minimum of 1.0 em ... against a letter tracking of 0.40 em ... never less than 2.5× the gap between two letters', CSS letter-spacing 0.40em / word-spacing 0.60em. Visual: tracking '+320/1000 em (0.32 em)', gap '+0.96 em minimum', ratio '≥ 3.0×', CSS 0.32em / 0.64em. Applications: '3× the letter tracking value, minimum'. Motion: 'a fixed 0.62em'. Verbal's own capital-O test returns a fifth answer. A printer holding this book has four mandates and a governance section swearing there is one.
contradictions.resolution: Visual §3.1.6 becomes the only statement of the rule anywhere: tracking 0.32 em, word gap 0.96 em absolute (CSS 0.32em letter-spacing + 0.64em word-spacing), ratio ≥3.0×. Delete the numbers from Verbal §6.1–6.2 and Applications §0.2 and replace both with a pointer. Change Motion's 0.62em to 0.64em. Demote the capital-O test to a labelled eyeball check, not a spec.

contradictions.issue: The two sections give incompatible launch ranges and nothing adjudicates. Strategy: 'Recommended launch cut: ~14 SKUs — the globe-coordinates tee (the hero), the navy hourglass tee, two wordmark tees ... two polos ... two shorts ... the washed-black jean.' Commercial: three garment types, six colourways, 320 units, with polos held to 'SS27, April', shorts to 'SS27, March', jeans to 'Year two', and the globe tee explicitly withdrawn — 'The globe tee with the Black Isle coordinates is a campaign, not a colourway — do not waste it as one of eight options in drop one.' Strategy makes that exact tee the launch hero and includes the jeans that two other sections prove cannot be made. Strategy also uses 'SKU' to mean colourway while Commercial uses it to mean colourway×size ('≈ 150 SKUs'), so the two numbers are not even in the same unit.
contradictions.resolution: Commercial wins — it is the only section that costed it. Cut Strategy §7.20's launch list entirely and replace with one line: 'Launch range is defined in Commercial §2.2. Strategy does not set it.' Then add a precedence order to the front matter: Commercial overrides on what gets made and when; Visual overrides on how anything looks; Verbal overrides on what anything is called.

contradictions.between: Strategy Pillar 1 & §7.10 vs Visual §3.2.1 vs Motion §2.3
contradictions.issue: Strategy states flatly 'No accent colour is ever introduced' and lists 'No accent colour' as prohibition 10. Visual then creates a role literally titled 'Accent (the only one)' — #54647E, 'Links, active states, data marks, the coordinate line, the one thing on a page allowed to be a colour.' Motion has 'the only saturated colour in the entire motion system ... That is the whole accent policy.' Worse, Visual opens §3.2.1 with 'Every colour has exactly one job. Colours do not move between roles' and then gives #54647E two jobs — the UI accent and a garment colourway (the 1600 SHORT).
contradictions.resolution: Rewrite the rule once as: 'The accent is #54647E. It is the only one and no second is ever added.' Strike 'No accent colour' from Strategy §7 and Pillar 1, replacing it with 'No accent beyond #54647E; C* 20 is the ceiling.' Then either drop the washed-denim short or accept, in writing, that the accent doubles as a garment and delete the one-job-per-colour sentence.

contradictions.between: Verbal §3.7 vs Applications §1.3 vs Applications §3.4 vs Commercial §3.4
contradictions.issue: Four different care instructions for the same garments, two of them mutually exclusive. Verbal care label: 'HANG DRY.' Applications care label block: 'TUMBLE DRY LOW'. Applications thank-you card: 'LINE DRY.' Commercial shrinkage disclosure: 'Hang dry. Do not tumble dry.' This is not a style inconsistency — a customer who tumble-dries a garment-dyed heavyweight per the sewn-in label and shrinks it has a claim, and the book's own §7.6 walks through the consumer law that makes it stick.
contradictions.resolution: One care block, authored once in Applications §1.3, reproduced nowhere else in full. Given garment-dyed heavyweight cotton the line is 'WASH COLD 30°. INSIDE OUT. HANG DRY. DO NOT TUMBLE DRY. COOL IRON — NOT ON PRINT.' Delete the competing blocks from Verbal §3.7 and the thank-you card and replace them with a cross-reference. Keep 'IT WILL FADE. THAT IS THE POINT.' as the one voice line beneath it.

contradictions.issue: Three specifications for one object, the swing tag. Verbal front: 'the lockup only. OT monogram above, OUR TIME wordmark below, EST. 2026 beneath.' Applications front: 'OT monogram, 26mm wide ... Nothing else. No tagline, no URL, no EST. 2026.' Two different fronts. Sizes: Applications '45 × 90mm portrait', '450gsm uncoated'; Visual 'Hang tag: 50 × 90 mm, 400 gsm uncoated'. Backs differ too — Verbal's has no QR and no handle, Applications' has both. This is the cheapest, most-touched physical item in the brand and the book specifies it three times without noticing.
contradictions.resolution: Applications §2.1–2.2 is the spec; it is the only version with a reasoned argument behind the format and the stock. Set 45 × 90mm, 450gsm uncoated everywhere. Delete Verbal §3.8 and Visual §3.6.2's hang-tag line, replacing both with a pointer. Then pick one front — the monogram alone is the stronger call, and it is the one with the reason attached.

contradictions.issue: Visual establishes the ground-assignment rule — navy and washed black are 'PAPER #DFDDDE' colourways, because 'a navy tee on #0F0F0F is a 1.12 : 1 silhouette' — and calls it 'a rule and not a preference'. Three later sections then instruct the founder to do exactly the forbidden thing. Lookbook pp.6–13: 'full-garment flat-lay (dead-on, soft top light, #0F0F0F ground)' for the whole range. Instagram §5.4: 'Dead-on, one garment' on 'near-black ground'. Commercial §5: 'flat-lay, dead-on, soft top light, near-black ground, per the art direction. Every colourway.' And drop one is navy tee, navy hoodie, washed-black sweatpant — four of six pieces Visual says must be shot on paper.
contradictions.resolution: Propagate the rule into every section that commissions a photograph. Add to Applications §5.4, §6.3 and Commercial's week 8–10 task: 'Ground per Visual §3.2.5 — dark colourways shoot on #DFDDDE. A product grid that mixes grounds is correct.' Then fix the drop-one shot list so the founder does not turn up to one session expecting one background.

contradictions.issue: Two different clock dials, both called the brand's second mark. Visual mandates 'OT at 12 — Mandatory. The monogram replaces XII. This is what makes it ours rather than a clip-art dial.' Motion builds a dial with the numerals 'I–XII' intact, 'XII heavy', as 'the hand', and the OT monogram sitting at the centre instead — 'R0 never rotates.' The packaging seal in Applications §3.1 uses Visual's version ('the Roman-numeral clock face with OT at 12'). So the sticker on the parcel and the animation on the site are different marks. Visual also writes the fixed time as '07:24' with a colon, in a book where Verbal §4.2 explains the colon is 'deliberately withheld'.
contradictions.resolution: Resolve in Visual's favour, because it is the printed asset: OT replaces XII on every appearance, and Motion's R1 runs I–XI plus the OT lozenge at twelve, which also gives the ring exactly one heavy moving element without needing a separate XII. Restate the fixed time as '0724' everywhere.

contradictions.between: Verbal §4.8 vs Strategy §7.20/§3 vs Visual §3.5.1 vs Commercial §0/§2.1
contradictions.issue: The range is counted three ways in a book whose thesis is single-source-of-truth. Verbal §4.8: 'Twenty-eight pieces, as counted from the current range', and the tables do total 28 (7+5+4+4+6+1+1). Strategy: 'roughly 31 colourways'. Visual §3.5.1: 'every one of the ~31 colourways'. Commercial: '~31 colourways ... ≈ 150 SKUs ... ≈ £39,000 of stock'. The £39,000 headline figure and the whole rationalisation argument are built on a count that the only section that actually enumerated the range says is 28.
contradictions.resolution: 28 is right — Verbal §4.8 is the only place anyone counted. Replace every '~31' with '28' and rerun Commercial §2.1's arithmetic (28 × 5 sizes = 140 SKUs, ≈ £36,000). Add one line to Commercial: 'Range size is whatever Verbal §4.8 lists. If that table and this section disagree, the table is right and this section is stale.'

contradictions.issue: Strategy's cheapest, do-it-now recommendation is that "'EST. 2026 · BLACK ISLE, SCOTLAND' appears on the neck label". Applications §1.2 forbids it: 'Artwork: OT monogram only. Not the wordmark. This is the single most important label decision in this section' — because thread cannot hold the wordmark's hairlines at 25mm and the word space would close, 'reproducing the OURTIME failure in a form that cannot be corrected without rebuying 500 labels.' Applications is right and Strategy's Level 1 is unbuildable at the neck.
contradictions.resolution: Strike the neck label from Strategy's Level 1 list. The place statement lives on the printed care label, the swing tag back and the site footer, all of which Applications already specifies and all of which are printed, not woven. Strategy Level 1 becomes: care label, swing tag, footer, bio, packing slip.

contradictions.between: Verbal §3.3 examples vs Commercial §1.2 blank list vs Strategy §4
contradictions.issue: Verbal calls the fabric line 'the single most persuasive sentence on the page' and rules 'if you do not know the gsm, ask the factory before you write the line. Do not guess.' It then guesses in its own examples: '380gsm loopback cotton', '240gsm piqué cotton', '320gsm cotton', '14oz rigid denim'. Commercial's chosen blanks are AS Colour 320gsm fleece and the 220gsm Chad Polo. Strategy separately demands the tee be 'genuinely heavyweight (240gsm+)' while costing it on a blank that is not. The section that bans invented numbers is populated entirely with invented numbers, and they contradict the buy.
contradictions.resolution: Strip every gsm from the Verbal examples and replace with bracketed placeholders — '[weight]gsm loopback cotton.' — with a standing note: these are filled from the supplier spec sheet after the wash test in Commercial weeks 3–5, not before. Then state the actual weights once, in one table, after samples land.

contradictions.issue: The sting's last frame is specified as 'Last frame = THE SETTLED FRAME (§6.1)', and §6.1 defines that frame as 'Beat index 0. XII at top. R2 tick 0 at top. R4 tooth 0 at top' rendered 'from the same canvas code with t = 0'. But frame 89 sits at 2966ms, three beats in — R1 has advanced 90°, so XII is at three o'clock and every geared ring is off its start position. As written the sting ends on a one-frame jump cut, and the claim that the settled frame 'can never drift from the animation' is false for the exact asset that most depends on it.
contradictions.resolution: Either make the sting 12 beats so the train genuinely realigns (too long), or — better — end it at beat three and redefine THE SETTLED FRAME as beat index 3 rather than 0, then re-derive the OG image, favicon, email header and reduced-motion frame from that same t. One composition, six jobs, one timestamp.

cliches.item: 'made for people in the unwatched middle of building something'
cliches.replace_with: 'Unwatched middle' is a phrase nobody has ever said out loud; it is the most machine-written construction in the book, and it sits in the one sentence the founder has to be able to repeat in a shop. The whole statement is 46 words with three subordinate clauses. Cut to something sayable: 'Washed, heavyweight clothing made on the Black Isle, for people doing the part of the work nobody is watching.' If he can't say it to a stranger without reading it, it isn't a positioning statement.

cliches.item: 'EARN EVERY SECOND.' — marked 'G · H · E · P · S' (every surface the brand owns)
cliches.replace_with: Strategy proves this line is a commodity — it links an Amazon print-on-demand sweatshirt and a UK label already running the same words — and then the tagline bank clears it for garments, hero, email, packaging and social, the Instagram bio ends on it, the thank-you card front IS it, and the drop email rotates it. The book disowns the line in section one and ships it on nine surfaces. Demote it to 'G' only, on one tee, and let 'THE HOURS SHOW.' carry the digital surfaces. If nothing else changes in this book, change this.

cliches.item: 'THE CLOCK IS TICKING.' rejected as 'Manufactured urgency. Ruled out at brand level.' — while 'TIME WON'T WAIT.' is cleared for G · H · E · S
cliches.replace_with: Same sentence, different wording. 'Time won't wait' is manufactured urgency with a full stop on it, and it is the copy printed on the 404. Either both go or neither does. Cut 'TIME WON'T WAIT.' and put 'THE WEATHER DOESN'T ASK.' on the 404 — it is the same idea, it is local, it is not a fridge magnet, and it is already in the bank.

cliches.item: 'KEEP YOUR OWN TIME.' / 'SET YOUR OWN HOUR.' / 'NOBODY HANDS YOU THE HOUR.' / 'NO ONE CLOCKS YOU IN.'
cliches.replace_with: Four lines saying one thing in one construction. This is the synonym-fan tell: a bank of 21 lines where a voice would have six. Keep 'NO ONE CLOCKS YOU IN.' — it is the only one with a working-life specific in it — and delete the other three. A brand with 21 taglines has none.

cliches.item: 'WE KEEP TIME. WE DON'T SELL IT.'
cliches.replace_with: The X-not-Y chiasmus is the single most reliable signature of generated copy, and this one is also untrue on its face: the About page it sits on is attached to a shop. Cut it. If the About page needs a line, use a fact — 'Eighteen hours of light in June. Six in December.'

cliches.item: 'WIND IT. WEAR IT.' — annotated 'sparingly; it is the closest to a joke we allow'
cliches.replace_with: A rhyme that means nothing (you do not wind a sweatshirt), and the annotation apologising for it is itself the tell — if a line needs a permission note, it has failed. Delete outright.

cliches.item: 'SECONDS ARE CHEAP. HOURS AREN'T.'
cliches.replace_with: Aphorism-generator output, and arguably backwards — an hour is sixty of the cheap thing. Replace with something the place gives you free: 'SIX HOURS OF LIGHT. USE THEM.' or, better, nothing.

cliches.item: 'Pillar 1 — Earned, not announced' / 'Pillar 3 — Our, not my' / 'Pillar 4 — Consistency is the product'
cliches.replace_with: Three of four pillar names are the same antithesis template, which is what a deck does when it has one idea and needs four boxes. Worse, only Pillar 2 is a proposition — Pillar 1 restates the aesthetic Visual already specifies, Pillar 3 restates the name, and Pillar 4 is a file-management policy wearing a pillar's clothes. Cut to two real pillars: 'Time you can feel' (the only differentiated claim) and 'Our, not my' (the only one that changes casting and copy). Move Pillar 4 into the ops checklist where it belongs, and let Pillar 1 live as the design rule it already is.

cliches.item: 'Consistency is the product'
cliches.replace_with: The product is a 320gsm cotton sweatshirt. Naming an artwork-repository policy as a brand pillar is the move a strategy deck makes when it wants to dignify admin, and it hands the founder a pillar he cannot express in a garment. Retitle it 'The pre-press gate' and file it under operations.

cliches.item: 'It is called THE MECHANISM' — alongside THE LEDGER, THE SETTLED FRAME, THE CORE, THE DROPS, THE 0300 SET, THE RESTRAINT BUDGET, THE HONEST HEADLINE
cliches.replace_with: Eight things given Proper Capitalised Names as if each were registrable IP. It reads as a book impressing itself. Keep THE LEDGER (it is the site's actual organising idea) and call the animation 'the mechanism', lowercase, like the object it is. Delete the rest of the naming.

cliches.item: 'THE CENTRE HOLDS'
cliches.replace_with: Yeats, inverted, unattributed, and the single most-reached-for line in motion design decks. The rule underneath it is good — the monogram never rotates. Name it what it does: 'THE MONOGRAM NEVER TURNS.'

cliches.item: 'MECHANISMS TICK, BODIES GLIDE'
cliches.replace_with: Another X/Y antithesis, and it obscures a rule that is genuinely the best technical call in the section. Rename to 'GEARS SNAP. ORBITS DON'T.' — same length, states the actual instruction, and a developer can check work against it.

cliches.item: 'Scarcity that is always on is not scarcity, it is a Shopify app.'
cliches.replace_with: Printed four times across four sections, near-verbatim, including once in the client brief it came from. A book that repeats its best line four times has one line. Keep it once, in Commercial §4.2 where the drop model is actually decided, and let the other three sections say 'no countdowns — see Commercial §4.2.'

cliches.item: 'It wins on all five tests:' … 'It is unsupervisable-proof.'
cliches.replace_with: A five-point rubric invented after the answer, to score the answer, plus a coined word that is not a word. This is the shape of a machine justifying its own output. Cut the rubric to the one claim that matters and is falsifiable: 'The founder never invents a name — he looks the colour up in a locked table.' Then go and test whether a customer can read 0600 as cream.

cliches.item: 'The brand has been half-doing this by accident.' / 'exactly the position OUR TIME is already in and does not yet know it' / 'nobody has said so out loud yet' / 'This is the part the brand most urgently does not have.'
cliches.replace_with: The same reveal-framing six times: here is the thing you already had and hadn't noticed. It is flattery architecture, and by the fourth repetition it reads as a tic rather than an insight. Keep one instance — the palette/landscape observation in Applications §5.1, which is the only one that is actually a discovery — and state the rest flat.

cliches.section: Passim (Strategy §7, Commercial §0, Verbal §6.3, Applications §4, Visual §3.6.4, Verbal §3.3)
cliches.item: 'The most useful page here.' / 'Section 2 is the most valuable page in this book.' / 'The single most important sentence in this entire document' / 'Read that first if nothing else' / 'the single highest-leverage decision in the document' / 'the single most persuasive sentence on the page' / 'the single most important label decision in this section'
cliches.replace_with: At least nine competing superlative self-rankings. When nine things are the most important, the founder — who is the one person this book exists for — has no hierarchy at all. Allow exactly one 'read this first' in the whole book (the single-source-of-truth rule), strip every other superlative, and let a one-page 'do these six things' summary carry the priority.

cliches.item: 'A price is a promise.'
cliches.replace_with: Mug slogan inside a costing section. The paragraph under it is excellent and concrete — 240gsm, collar rib that survives washing, a print that doesn't crack. Delete the aphorism and lead with the specifics.

cliches.item: 'Specificity is what travels; genericism is what stays home.' / 'be from somewhere, be for everyone.'
cliches.replace_with: Two LinkedIn aphorisms in one table cell, one of them coining 'genericism'. The Queens/ALD evidence in the same row does the job on its own. Cut both sentences.

cliches.item: 'Nobody else can print 57.5878° N, 4.2383° W and mean it.'
cliches.replace_with: Anyone can print it; that is what a coordinate is. The claim is rhetoric standing where an argument should be, and it is load-bearing for the book's central bet. Replace with the thing that is actually unfakeable: 'Anyone can print the coordinates. Only someone who lives there can shoot the range in that light, on those days, all year.'

cliches.item: 'is one of roughly none' / 'is one of approximately none'
cliches.replace_with: The same joke, twice, in two sections, in slightly different words — which is exactly the failure mode the book is written to fix, reproduced in its own prose. Say it once, in Strategy, and let the other two sections point at it.

cliches.item: The 600-word researched provenance of the Capaldi titles — Billy Hanshaw, Moffat's quote, Cinema 4D, the Seal of Rassilon
cliches.replace_with: Genuinely well-sourced and completely unusable: §5.4 then forbids the reference from ever surfacing publicly. A non-technical founder is being handed a footnoted television-history essay about an animation he can never mention. Cut to four lines — concentric rings, meshed counter-rotation, lock-and-hold timing, one object across print and screen — and move the research to an appendix.

cliches.item: Preheader 'Twenty-eight pieces. Seven garments. One drop.' — under a mechanics rule reading 'Numerals: Digits, always. "24", "0600", "2026". Never "twenty-four".'
cliches.replace_with: The section breaks its own rule in its own worked example, three lines below stating it. '28 pieces. 7 garments. One drop.' And that preheader also contradicts the six-colourway drop one — it is advertising the full range as a single launch.

gaps: The founder's actual connection to the Black Isle is never established, and the entire positioning rests on it. Applications §5.1 raises exactly the right doubt — 'the brand should not claim the Black Isle unless there is a real connection to it ... If he does not, the coordinates are a second fabrication and should be dropped rather than defended' — and then Strategy builds the whole strategic bet on top of the unanswered question. This is the first thing to close, before anything is printed. One question to the cousin: does he live there, is he from there, or did he pick it? The answer changes the book.

The domain and handle are never chosen. Every section prints a placeholder — 'OURTIME.[TLD]', '@[handle]' — on the swing tag back, the thank-you card, the lookbook back cover, the email footer and the care block. Commercial §7.1 proves ourtime.com and ourtime.co.uk belong to a Match Group dating service with 190,000 UK members and says 'pick something searchable'; nobody picks. Nothing physical can be ordered until this one string exists, and it is the string the QR code redirects to.

Nothing sets a total capital requirement. Money is committed in five places — ~£10,800 of stock, £450–800 of type licences, £205+ trade mark, £150–600 insurance, woven labels, care labels, swing tags, a deboss die, three separate strike-offs at £100–200 each, lookbook print, a paid QR redirect service, Shopify at £19–25/month — and no section adds them up. A founder cannot decide whether he can start, and Commercial §5's gate ('you have the full cost of the buy in the bank plus 20% contingency') is unusable because the buy is only one line of it.

Precedence between the five sections is never declared. Visual opens with 'Where this document and any existing artwork disagree, this document wins' — but says nothing about the other four sections, and it is Visual that reopens the OVERTIME disposal decision Strategy and Commercial both closed. A book written to end 'several versions of the truth' has five documents and no order of authority.

Who owns the master artwork folder. Visual Rule 3.0.4 specifies 'One cloud folder, one owner, read-only to everyone else' and never names the owner — and the owner is the whole mechanism. Same for who holds the trade mark once filed, and whether the website builder's involvement is paid, equity or a favour. Every governance rule in the book depends on a named person and no person is named.

Photography is specified three incompatible ways and budgeted at zero. Visual demands a tethered 50–85mm at f/8 on a levelled rig, grey card at 5200K, matte plaster ground at LRV 3% and sheen ≤5 GU, one master capture per garment cropped to five ratios. Applications says everything is 'achievable on a phone'. Commercial schedules the shoot in weeks 8–10 with no budget line, no named photographer and no kit list. Decide: hire someone for two days, or write the phone-realistic spec. Do not ship both.

Wholesale is foreclosed by the price architecture and nobody says so. Strategy Level 3 proposes 'a physical presence or stockist in Inverness' and Commercial §7.1 suggests registering class 35 for retail services — but at a 2.01× multiple on the tee, a standard 50% wholesale discount prices it at £25 against a £24.85 landed cost. The book proposes stockists in one section and makes them loss-making in another without either noticing.

The falsification test has no branch. Strategy proposes a genuinely good one — 'if, at launch, the units that actually sell are the loud graphic back-prints to 17-year-olds who have never heard of the Black Isle ... then the brand is a graphics label and the place is decoration. Watch the sell-through by SKU in the first two drops. That is the test.' It then never says what changes if the test fails. A test with no consequence attached is a rhetorical device, not a decision.

The navy is never picked, and drop one depends on it. Visual §3.2.2a rules the two navies 'may never appear in the same photograph, flat-lay set, or product grid', lists the choice as Open Item 2, and defers it. Commercial's drop one is navy tee plus navy zip hoodie — the exact pair — and every campaign image will want them together. Pick one navy before the buy, not after.

Returns logistics are absent from a book that gets returns law right. No return address, no decision on who inspects, no restocking process, no decision on whether a returned garment gets a new hand-tied waxed-cotton tag (it must — the string is cut to remove it), and no line for any of it in the contribution model that already only clears ~£15 on a single-tee order at a 25–30% return rate.

Where the stock lives and who packs it. £9,000 of inventory appears once, inside the insurance paragraph ('probably won't cover £9,000 of stock in a spare room either'), and is never actually decided as a fulfilment question: storage, packing station, what happens to dispatch when the founder is away for a week, and whether 'pack and post daily' survives a full-time job.

Nothing decides how the customer shops. Verbal builds the 24-hour index but never resolves whether the shop's product title is '0600 CREW', 'Crewneck — Cream' or both; whether the URL slug is the hour; what a marketplace or Vinted listing reads, where '0600 CREW' is unsearchable; or what the size dropdown does. The naming system stops at the swing tag and never reaches the shop.
unsupported_claims: 'UK streetwear in 2026 is a roughly £8.6bn market growing ~4.9% year on year, and the growth has shifted from explosive to premium and sustainable' — one citation, to a sourcing-industry content site, with no methodology and no definition of 'streetwear'. The 'premium and sustainable' half of the claim is doing the strategic work ('the winners now win on story and make') and has no evidence behind it at all.

'Corteiz's Royale heavyweight tee retails around $63–85 (StockX)'. StockX is a resale marketplace; that is a secondary-market price, not a retail price, and it is the anchor for the recommended £45–55 tee band. Category error on the book's most consequential number.

'Cole Buxton hoodies are £175' (Strategy §4) against Commercial's own verified table — '£75 tee, £139 hoodie, £159 zip hoodie' and '£98–£175 at Flannels'. Strategy takes the top of a third-party retailer's range and reports it as the brand's price, then uses it to justify a £95–110 hoodie that Commercial prices at £85.

'68% of Gen Z workers say they'd take a pay cut for better work-life balance, and 42% have turned down promotions to avoid the stress' — cited to an aggregator, with no named survey, sample size or country. Almost certainly US data, used to justify a UK brand-voice decision.

'the longest day in 2026 runs 18 hours 7 minutes and the shortest 6 hours 41 minutes' — sourced to a timeanddate page for Inverness filtered to June, which cannot contain the December figure. The precision to the minute is spurious without stating the sunrise/sunset definition used, and the same fact appears as 'nine hours of usable winter daylight' in Visual §3.4.3, 'up around 09:00 and down around 15:30' in Visual §3.5.3, and 'done by half three' in Applications §5.1. Four numbers for the fact the book calls the brand's entire thesis.

'Finisterre ... turning over roughly £24m by 2023' — cited to a magazine feature and Wikipedia. Company turnover is a Companies House fact; Wikipedia is not a source for it, and this figure is the proof that the whole remote-place strategy is commercially viable.

'Chanonry Point ... is among the best places in Europe to watch bottlenose dolphins from land' — a tourism-board claim cited to Wikipedia and a tourism marketing body, and immediately irrelevant, since Visual §3.5.3 bans photographing the dolphins.

AS Colour blank costs: 'The 50+ price is consistently 62.5% of the 1–9 price ... so where the 50+ tier wasn't displayed I've applied that ratio and marked it.' The hero tee's £16.25 is inferred, not observed — and it is the single largest cost line in the £8,956 drop-one buy and in every margin figure in §1.3 and §8, where it appears unflagged. Compounding it, 'whether AS Colour's displayed prices are ex-VAT' is itself listed as unverified, a 20% swing on the same number.

Commercial §2.2 costs both drop-one tees at £24.85, the two-print-position figure, when both are back-print-only per the range description and §1.4's own fix is 'One print position, not two.' The buy is over-costed by roughly £490 in the section the book calls its most valuable page — and the §1.3 table also carries an unedited artefact, 'Sweatpants ... 2.43% → 2.43×', in a column of money.

'if a customer wrecks a garment following no instructions at all, the liability sits with the brand under the General Product Safety Regulations.' GPSR governs product safety, not care instructions or garment damage. Stated confidently, wrong, and used to push the founder toward a paid licence.

'Decorative matter making up 7% or less of the product is excluded — which is why a screen print does not need declaring.' The 7% allowance in the fibre-composition rules concerns fibres, not inks; a screen print is out of scope for a different reason entirely. Right conclusion, wrong law, in a section a founder will quote to a supplier.

Applications §3.3.3 heads the free-type table 'All OFL-licensed: free for commercial use, including on garments, with no merchandise restriction' and then lists Switzer, which is a Fontshare release under its own terms, not OFL. Asserting 'no merchandise restriction' for it — in the same section that correctly warns merchandise licences are 'a real and commonly-breached restriction' — is the exact exposure the section exists to prevent. Archivo Expanded Black Italic's availability as a static style also needs checking, not assuming.

Every type price is specific and uncited: 'Druk Wide ~£95–190 / style', 'GT America ~£50–70 / style', 'Realistic launch kit: 4–6 styles total, ≈ £450–£800 all-in', 'Monument Extended (Pangram Pangram, ~£120 family)', 'Neue Montreal (~£100 family)'. Pangram Pangram in particular does not price as a flat family fee.

'UK IPO £205 for the first class, £60 per additional class ... This was the first trade mark fee rise since 1998' — cited to a law-firm blog. The 'first rise since 1998' claim is doubtful and both numbers are ones a founder will spend against.

'Overtime Sports Inc., founded 2016 ... sells apparel under its own logos and branding' followed by 'I have not been able to confirm from the registers whether Overtime Sports holds UK or EU marks in class 25. Someone must check.' A trade-mark risk flagged and not checked is not advice, it is a liability note. The same is true of the core name: no register search was run for OUR TIME or OURTIME in class 25, and the book's whole legal position rests on one being run later.

Product liability insurance given as three overlapping ranges from broker marketing pages — '£150–£600/year', 'basic cover in low-risk textiles can be £50–£150', 'clothing shops commonly pay under £90/year for £2m of public liability'. Three different answers to one question, none quoted for this business.

Returns benchmarks: 'roughly 30%, and "poor fit" is the number one reason — with apparel benchmarks clustering in the mid-20s and 56% of apparel sellers reporting 30%+' — three numbers from one trade-news link, the 56% with no named survey behind it. And 'UK fashion & accessories AOV was £91.53 in May 2026' is IRP Commerce's own client network, not a UK market figure, presented as the target to beat.

'roughly 3–5% dimensional change happens during dyeing, leaving typically 1–3% residual shrinkage' — cited to a supplier's own blog, and then written into a customer-facing legal disclosure as 'expect up to a further 3%'. That sentence is explicitly framed as 'evidence you disclosed the characteristic'. It needs to come from the wash test in Commercial weeks 3–5, not from a blog.

'He has £60–£120 of genuinely discretionary clothing money a month and he spends it in concentrated bursts' — an invented persona economics figure with no source, sitting directly above the price table it justifies.

Visual §3.2.3 asserts 'Discharge will not give you #FAF6F6 on #141B2C navy — reactive navy dyes discharge to tan/pink' while Applications §4.2 establishes that garment-dyed and pigment-dyed cloth resists discharge entirely and that nobody has yet asked the blank supplier which it is. Visual is issuing a confident technical conclusion from a premise Applications says is unknown. The same table also ships '16-3850 TCX? — use 15-4502 TCX Silver / confirm' — a literal question mark in a supplier-facing spec.

The Instagram ratio '40% product · 30% location · 20% people · 10% mechanism/graphic' and the rule 'Never let two flat-lays sit adjacent' are stated as rules with no basis given, alongside 'Realistic cadence: three posts a week' — all three are plausible and all three are asserted.
strongest:
"Mapping the existing heavy/thin logo pair onto the two halves of the name's arc, and then enforcing that mapping as a rule in every medium. Verbal §0 and Strategy §2 state it: 'The thin wordmark carries process copy. The heavy monogram carries arrival.' Motion §2.1 reproduces it inside one ring — 'R1 sets I–XI in the thin wordmark weight and XII in the heavy monogram weight' — with 'R0 never rotates. The monogram is the fixed point and time moves around it.' Visual §3.3.1 derives the type system from it and bans mid-weights as 'the enemy'.

This is the only idea in the book that is genuinely brand thinking rather than decoration, for three reasons. First, it is derived from an asset the label already owns instead of invented — the cousin made that heavy/thin pair by instinct, and the book's job here is to notice what he did and make it a rule, which is the correct relationship between a brand book and a founder who is already half-right. Second, it resolves a real incoherence rather than papering over it: 'EARN EVERY SECOND' and 'OUR TIME' genuinely do pull in opposite directions, and rather than picking one, the arc makes the tension the structure — 'they are a before and an after, and the whole brand is the sentence that joins them.' Third, and this is the test a brand idea has to pass, it is checkable on any surface by someone with no design training. Is there more than one heavy thing here? Then it is wrong. That single question governs a garment, a page, a still frame and a three-second Reel, and it needs no taste to apply.

One warning that goes with the praise: the section that most needed this idea ignored it. The tagline bank in Verbal §5 never sorts its 21 lines into process and arrival. If the arc were applied there, nine of them would fall out on contact, because they are neither."
weakest:
"The 24-hour colour index (Verbal §4). It is the one wholly new system the book invents, it is the most expensive thing in the book to reverse — it goes into the SKU scheme, the internal neck label, the swing tag, the shop's product titles and the merchandising sets — and its central premise is almost certainly false at point of sale.

The premise is that '0600 CREW' will read as cream because the colour 'looks like that hour on the Black Isle'. It won't. Nobody can distinguish 0500 taupe from 0700 tan by time of day ('Warmer than 0600 by an hour'), the mapping is unfalsifiable, and the section fails its own stated objection to a bare numbered index — it rejects '001, 002, 003' because 'the numbers carry no meaning — 014 tells you nothing, so nobody remembers it', and 0600 also tells you nothing unless you have read a ledger the customer will never see. The shop has to show '0600 CREW — Cream' anyway, which means the hour is a decoration sitting on top of the real name, not a replacement for it. It is also unsearchable on Vinted and Depop — the resale presence Strategy §4 says is strategically load-bearing — and it collapses precisely where the book most celebrates it: once six garments share 0300, the hour has stopped naming anything and become a colour synonym with worse recall. The system also writes a rule for year two before drop one exists ('0000 is reserved. Midnight is held for the annual anniversary piece only'), which is the tell that it was designed for elegance rather than use.

What would fix it: demote the hour from the product name to a collection layer, and validate it before it is woven into 500 labels. Primary name stays the plain thing a customer can search and say — 'CREW — Cream'. The hour rides alongside as an index mark, in the mono, in the way the Ledger already uses index marks: 'CREW — Cream · 0600'. The sets still work ('THE 0300 SET' is genuinely good merchandising and survives intact), the SKU scheme is untouched, the founder still gets lookup-not-judgement naming, and the neck label still carries the hour as the detail only the owner finds. Then run the actual test before committing: show twelve people the six launch colours and the hour table and ask them to match. If they can't, the hour was never a name — it was a mood, and it belongs where moods belong, inside the copy."
